# Bug Report: App crashes when device language is set to Turkish

**Title:** Crash on launch/startup when device language is Turkish (tr-TR)

**Severity:** Critical (crash, blocks use for all Turkish-locale users)

**Platform:** iOS / Android [specify versions]
**App version:** [x.y.z (build)]
**Device:** [model, OS version]
**Reproducibility:** 100% with device language set to Turkish

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Go to Settings > General > Language & Region (iOS) or Settings > System > Languages (Android).
2. Set the device language to Türkçe (Turkish).
3. Launch the app.
4. Navigate to [screen/feature where crash occurs, if not at launch].

## Expected Result
The app launches and displays correctly with Turkish locale formatting and text, or falls back to a default language without crashing.

## Actual Result
The app crashes immediately [or: when opening X]. [Attach crash log / stack trace.]

## Stack Trace
```
[Paste crash log here. Look for the top application frame, e.g., a force unwrap, failed key lookup, or parse exception.]
```

## Suspected Cause
Turkish has dotted and dotless forms of "i" (I/İ and ı/i). Locale-sensitive case conversion can change string identity in ways that break code assuming ASCII casing. Likely causes:
- `toUpperCase()` / `toLowerCase()` called without an explicit locale (e.g., `"id".toUpperCase()` yields `"İD"` under tr-TR), producing keys that don't match stored values.
- Enum or dictionary lookups built from case-converted strings returning nil/null, followed by a force unwrap or `!` operator.
- Date, number, or currency parsing with the default locale, causing format mismatches (e.g., decimal separators or `dd.MM.yyyy` patterns).
- Sorting or comparison using locale-aware collation that differs from expected order.

## Suggested Fix
- Use locale-invariant case conversion for internal identifiers: `Locale.ROOT` in Java/Kotlin, `uppercased(with: Locale(identifier: "en_US_POSIX"))` or ASCII-only handling in Swift, or `toUpperCase(Locale.ENGLISH)`.
- Store and compare machine-readable values (keys, enum raw values, API fields) without locale-dependent transformations.
- Use `Locale.current` only for user-facing display formatting.
- Replace force unwraps and `!!` on lookups with safe handling and a fallback.
- Add a unit test that runs with `Locale("tr", "TR")` covering identifier parsing, enum mapping, and date/number formatting.

## Additional Notes
- Confirm whether the crash also occurs with other locales that have special casing (e.g., Azerbaijani `az`, Lithuanian `lt`).
- Check whether the issue appears only in the Turkish UI language or also when only the region is set to Turkey.

# Postmortem: Checkout and API outage, expired TLS certificate

**Date:** [date]
**Duration:** 40 minutes (14:12 to 14:52 UTC)
**Severity:** SEV-1
**Author:** [name]

## What happened

At 14:12 UTC, the wildcard certificate for `*.example.com` expired. Browsers and mobile clients started rejecting connections to the public API, the web app, and checkout. Internal services talking over the same hostnames were affected too. Our uptime monitor paged at 14:14, but the on-call engineer first assumed it was a load balancer problem and spent about six minutes restarting ingress pods before checking the cert.

Once we confirmed the expiry, we issued a new certificate from our CA, pushed it to the load balancers, and confirmed traffic recovered by 14:52. Most of the delay came from the renewal not being automated for this particular cert.

## Why it happened

The cert was issued by hand about a year ago, before we moved DNS and TLS management into the cert-manager setup. It was never added to cert-manager, so nothing renewed it. The expiry reminder emails went to a distribution list that nobody has been reading since the team reorg in the spring.

## Impact

- Roughly 40 minutes of full outage for web and API traffic
- Checkout failed for the whole window. We're still pulling numbers from the payments side, but early estimates put lost orders in the low thousands.
- Two partner integrations got errors and will likely ask for a credit.

## What went well

- The alert fired within two minutes.
- Once someone looked at the cert, the fix was quick. The new cert was live about eight minutes after we started on it.
- Status page updates went out on time.

## What went poorly

- We spent too long on the ingress theory before checking the certificate. The first thing the runbook says to check is cert expiry, and nobody followed it.
- The reminder emails went to a list nobody watches.
- We had no inventory of certs outside cert-manager, so we didn't know this one existed until it broke.

## Action items

1. Move every certificate under the `example.com` zone into cert-manager, with renewal at 30 days before expiry. Owner: platform team, due in two weeks.
2. Add a monitor that alerts at 30 and 7 days before any cert expires, sent to the on-call channel and not email. Owner: [name], due Friday.
3. Update the outage runbook so checking cert expiry comes first for any TLS-related symptom. Owner: [name], due next week.
4. Audit the DNS and cert inventory and clean up the old distribution lists in the reminder configs. Owner: [name], due end of the month.
5. Draft a credit response for the two affected partners. Owner: [name], due tomorrow.

## `--dry-run`

Shows what a command would do without doing it. Nothing is written, deleted, moved, or sent. The output lists each change the command would have made, one per line, so you can check it before running the real thing.

```
tool sync --dry-run
```

Example output:

```
would create   deploy/config.yaml
would update   deploy/app.env
would delete   deploy/old-cache/
3 changes planned, 0 applied
```

### Notes

- Dry-run still reads your files and config, and it still contacts remote services for lookups like auth checks or listing existing resources. It just doesn't make changes.
- The plan can go stale. If something changes between your dry run and the real run, the real run may do something different. For anything important, look at the plan again right before you commit to it.
- Dry-run exits with status `0` if the plan builds successfully, even when it lists changes. If it hits an error while planning, it exits non-zero, the same as a real run would.
- Combining `--dry-run` with `--force` is allowed, but `--force` has no effect on the output. It only matters when the real run is executed.

## Connection Pooling

The client now supports connection pooling, which reuses open database connections instead of creating a new one for every query. This reduces connection latency and lowers the load on your database server, especially under concurrent workloads.

**What's new**

- Pools are created automatically when you connect, with sensible defaults for size and idle timeout.
- Configure the minimum and maximum pool size, idle timeout, and connection lifetime.
- Connections are validated before reuse, so stale or dropped connections are replaced automatically.
- Pool statistics (active, idle, and waiting connections) are available for monitoring.

**Upgrade notes**

- Pooling is enabled by default. To keep the previous one-connection-per-query behavior, set `pooling.enabled = false`.
- Applications that hold connections open for long periods should release them when finished so they return to the pool.

Setting Up a Static Site with a Custom Domain

Launching a static site is one of the fastest ways to get a project online, and it costs very little to run. In this tutorial, you'll build a simple site with plain HTML, CSS, and a bit of JavaScript, then publish it on free static hosting. Finally, you'll connect your own domain name so visitors can reach it at an address you control. By the end, you'll have a live, fast, HTTPS-secured site under your own branding.

A typical web application separates its concerns into distinct tiers. Clients (browsers or mobile apps) send HTTP requests to an application server, which handles business logic, authentication, and API routing. That server is typically fronted by a load balancer or reverse proxy such as Nginx to distribute traffic and terminate TLS. PostgreSQL serves as the system of record, storing relational data with transactional guarantees, while Redis sits alongside it as an in-memory cache, holding frequently read data, session state, and computed results to reduce database load and latency. The application follows a cache-aside pattern: it checks Redis first, falls back to Postgres on a miss, and then populates the cache, with entries expiring via TTLs or explicit invalidation when the underlying rows change. Background workers can process long-running or asynchronous jobs from a queue, and the whole stack is usually containerized so each component can be deployed, scaled, and monitored independently.

If you've got a static site sitting on your laptop and want it living at your own domain, this is about the easiest weekend project you can do. You don't need a server, you don't need to know Docker, and you probably already have most of what you need. A static site is just HTML, CSS, and maybe a bit of JavaScript, and a host like GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Cloudflare Pages will serve it for free. The only fiddly part is pointing your domain at the host, and that's mostly copying a couple of DNS records into your registrar's settings. This guide walks through the whole thing: getting the files up, connecting the domain, and turning on HTTPS so the little padlock shows up.

Rate limits are enforced per API key at 100 requests per minute. Each key may send up to 100 requests within any rolling 60-second window. Requests beyond this limit are rejected with HTTP status `429 Too Many Requests` until the window frees capacity. Each response includes the headers `X-RateLimit-Limit` (the maximum of 100), `X-RateLimit-Remaining` (requests left in the current window), and `X-RateLimit-Reset` (the Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the window resets). When you receive a `429` response, wait until the time indicated by `X-RateLimit-Reset` before retrying, and consider exponential backoff to avoid repeated rejections. Limits apply separately to each API key, so distributing traffic across multiple keys increases total throughput, subject to your account's terms.

```python
# Retry policy: exactly three attempts.
#
# The function makes up to three attempts in total (one initial call plus
# two retries) before giving up and raising the last error.
#
# Why three:
# - Most transient failures (brief network blips, connection resets, lock
#   contention, rate-limit windows) clear within a few seconds, so two
#   retries cover the large majority of recoverable cases.
# - Retrying more than that adds little success probability while
#   lengthening latency for the caller and increasing load on a service
#   that is already struggling.
# - Fewer than three leaves too little room for a second transient failure
#   to clear, which causes avoidable errors to surface to users.
# - Retries use exponential backoff between attempts so that a recovering
#   dependency is not hit with a burst of immediate retries.
#
# The limit is a fixed constant rather than an unbounded loop so that
# failures are bounded in time and cannot hang the caller indefinitely.
# Non-retryable errors (for example, validation or authentication failures)
# are raised immediately and do not consume retry attempts.
```

Mostly so it can show you things near you. If you're looking for a coffee shop, a bus stop, or a nearby event, the app needs to know roughly where you are to give you useful results. You can say no and the app will still work. You'll just have to type in your city or address yourself. You can also change this anytime in your phone's settings under Privacy or Location.

Remote work isn't what makes juniors worse. What hurts them is losing the ambient learning that used to happen for free. Overhearing a senior debug a production issue, watching how someone reads a messy codebase, or asking a quick question across the desk built judgment faster than any onboarding doc. Remote teams can replicate that, but only if they do it on purpose: pair programming, recorded design reviews, public Slack channels instead of DMs, and explicit mentorship time. Teams that treat juniors as a deliberate investment rarely see a gap. Teams that just ship them a laptop and hope for the best usually do.

Early on, my first manager told me that when I didn't know something, I should say so out loud and then say how I'd find out. I expected that admitting ignorance would make me look junior, but it did the opposite. People trusted my estimates more because they knew I'd flag what I was guessing at, and I stopped wasting days pretending to understand requirements I hadn't actually grasped.

The follow-up mattered just as much: "Say it, then go find out" became my default for the next decade. It turned a vague sense of inadequacy into a concrete next step, and it made me the person others came to when they needed a straight answer about what was known and what wasn't.

Quit social media for a year and honestly the biggest thing I noticed was how much mental space it was taking up without me realizing. like I'd pick up my phone to check one thing and 40 minutes later I'd be somewhere I didn't mean to be, feeling vaguely worse about my life and not even sure why. the first month was weird, kept reaching for the app out of habit. by month four it just stopped being a thing I thought about.

not saying everyone should do it. I still miss some stuff, like a couple friends who only really talked on there, and I had to be more intentional about keeping in touch. but I got a bunch of books read and started actually calling people instead of liking their posts. would do it again.

College isn't for everyone, and it's fair to question the cost. But the "waste of money" framing usually ignores what a degree actually does for people. Graduates tend to earn substantially more over their lifetimes, face lower unemployment rates, and have access to fields like medicine, engineering, and law that require credentials. The degree is also a signal to employers that you can commit to a long project and finish it.

That said, the value depends heavily on the field, the school, and how much debt you take on. Someone who graduates with little debt and a clear career path is in a very different position from someone who borrows heavily for a major with weak job prospects. The better question is whether a specific college education makes sense for a specific person, not whether college is a waste of money in general.

Plenty of people do find college worth the cost, but the answer depends a lot on the field, the price, and what a person plans to do with the degree. Someone going into nursing, engineering, or teaching usually has a clear path to a job that pays back the investment, and many fields simply require the credential to get in the door. The real problem is that students often borrow heavily without a plan, or pick a costly program with weak job prospects. Those are fair criticisms of how college is sometimes approached, but they point toward choosing carefully, not skipping it altogether.

Cheaper routes like community college transfers, in-state public schools, and employer tuition assistance can cut the cost dramatically while keeping most of the benefit. Before anyone decides college is a waste, it's worth looking at what they actually want to do and working backward from there.

I once lost a full week to a bug that turned out to be a single misplaced assumption. Our service would occasionally return stale data, but only on one machine in the cluster, and only after a deploy. I rebuilt the cache layer twice, read every line of the serialization code, and convinced myself the problem was clock skew. The real cause was a config file that a startup script silently rewrote with the default timezone, so that node read its TTLs in local time while the rest of the fleet used UTC. The lesson I took away is to diff the effective runtime config on every node before touching any application code.

that said i don't want to go back to a wall of cubicles either. the answer is probably a mix. a few people who need quiet get actual rooms, the rest of us get desks that aren't in a fishbowl. bring back the option, not the mandate.

Learning to cook in my thirties was the best decision I made for my health and my wallet. I started with one dish I could make on repeat, a basic tomato sauce, and built from there. Mistakes were part of it. I burned plenty of garlic and undercooked my share of chicken, but each failure taught me something about heat, timing, and seasoning.

What surprised me most was how much patience mattered more than talent. Nobody expects you to nail a braise on the first try, and grocery shopping with a plan makes everything easier. If you're starting now, pick three recipes you actually want to eat and make them until you don't need to look at the instructions anymore.

I used to think saving was mostly about cutting lunches and skipping vacations. *The Psychology of Money* by Morgan Housel changed that. His argument that behavior matters more than knowledge made me see that my biggest money problems came from wanting more than I needed and from chasing the next move instead of staying put. The chapter on "enough" stuck with me most, and I've started measuring my finances against what I want my life to feel like rather than against what others have.

I read The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel a few years ago, and it shifted how I think about spending. I used to measure my finances against other people's lifestyles, which kept me chasing things I didn't really want. Housel's point that wealth is the money you don't spend, and that getting rich is different from staying rich, made me stop comparing and start asking what I actually needed.

The idea that stuck with me most is that good financial decisions often depend more on behavior than on intelligence. Saving steadily, avoiding debt, and giving yourself room to absorb bad luck matter more than finding the perfect investment. I still don't understand markets better than most people, but I sleep better, and I think that's the real return.

Kids under 12 don't need their own phones, and the research on early smartphone use is giving parents good reasons to wait. Kids this age are still building the self-control, attention, and sleep habits that a phone can easily disrupt, and the constant pull of notifications, games, and social feeds tends to crowd out time for reading, play, and face-to-face friendships. Many 10- and 11-year-olds also aren't ready for the social pressure that comes with group chats and public posting, where a single bad moment can follow them for years.

That said, the answer depends on the child and the family. A kid who needs to reach a parent after school, or who's walking home alone, may reasonably have a basic phone with no internet, no social apps, and clear limits. The problem is less about the device itself than about handing over unrestricted internet access before a child has the maturity to handle it. Parents who wait, set firm rules, and talk openly with their kids about online life are giving them a much better start than any fixed age could.

Switching to Linux was the best computer decision I've made in years. Windows kept nudging me toward things I didn't ask for: ads in the Start menu, forced updates that rebooted my machine mid-work, and telemetry I couldn't fully turn off. On Linux, the system does what I tell it to, and I can see exactly what's running and why. My package manager handles installs and updates in one place, so I'm no longer hunting through random installers and bundled toolbars.

The transition was smoother than I expected. Most of my daily work happens in a browser and a terminal anyway, and the apps I did need had good alternatives or ran fine through Wine and Proton. Games were the biggest question mark, but Steam's Proton support has improved a lot, and plenty of titles now run as well as they do on Windows. I still keep a dual-boot option for the few things that won't cooperate, but I haven't touched it in months.

I walked into a final-round interview at a small design firm, and the hiring manager spent the first ten minutes scrolling through my portfolio on his phone, muttering "mm-hm" without looking up. When I asked about the role, he said, "Honestly? We just need someone to fix the logo on our coffee cups," then asked me to sketch a new one on the spot. I did, because I needed the job, and he photographed it, said "cute," and ended the interview by asking whether I could start Monday without pay for the first month.

I still think about how I kept smiling the whole time. I walked out into the parking lot, sat in my car, and laughed until I cried. The best part was the follow-up email a week later, which opened with "Hope you're well!" and offered me a "fun little freelance gig" at a rate that would have covered about one coffee cup's worth of ink.

My startup tried to solve a problem I was sure everyone had: scheduling shared household chores. We spent eight months building it, and the beta users liked it, but almost none of them came back after the first week. The mistake was mine. I fell in love with the product's features and never checked whether anyone felt the pain sharply enough to change their habits. Most couples I talked to said the chores were annoying, not that they were breaking their relationships, so they never had a reason to adopt a new tool.

The biggest lesson was to test the urgency of the problem before writing a line of code. Now I ask people what they did the last time the problem bit them, and whether they paid to fix it. If they can't name a recent example or a dollar amount, I treat that as a warning sign. I'd rather learn that in two weeks of interviews than in two years of building.

Spent two years building a meal planning app that I was sure people would pay for. They signed up, poked around, and then almost none of them came back after the first week. I spent most of that time polishing features and assumed the problem was discovery or pricing. It wasn't. The real issue was that I never confirmed people had the specific pain I was solving, and the ones who did already had a workaround that was good enough.

If I started over, I'd spend the first month talking to potential users and asking them to show me how they currently handle the problem, instead of asking whether they'd like my solution. I'd also set a hard deadline for a go or no-go decision based on retention, not sign-ups. The failure cost me time and some savings, but the lesson was worth it, and I'm already applying it to my next idea.

Picking up woodworking this past year saved me more than I expected. Some nights I'd just go down to the garage and sand the same piece of walnut for an hour, and my head would finally go quiet. Nothing about it was urgent. The wood didn't care how my week went, and I didn't have to be good at it to show up. I've made a lopsided cutting board, a wobbly stool, and a shelf that's slightly out of level, and I love every one of them more than anything I bought at a store.

If you're going through something hard right now, my advice is to find a small, slow thing with your hands and give yourself permission to be bad at it. You don't need a goal or a finished product. Showing up to the bench, or the kitchen, or the garden, is enough.

Honestly I think a lot of it was that you couldn't save whenever you wanted. You had one life, a limited number of continues, and if you died near the end of a level you got sent back to the start with nothing. That made every run feel like it mattered. Nowadays if a boss wipes you, you just reload a checkpoint 30 seconds back and try again, which is great, but it also means the stakes are gone.

The other thing is that you didn't have guides or wikis. You figured out where the hidden block was by bumping into every wall, and you learned enemy patterns by dying to them over and over. Being stuck for an afternoon was normal, and beating something felt like you'd earned it because nobody had told you how. I think some of the "it was harder" feeling is really just that we had less information and more time to kill, and that combination made the difficulty feel bigger than it probably was.

Title: I got lost on the trail for three hours. Here's how I found it again.

Okay, so this is a bit embarrassing, but I want to share it in case it saves someone else from the same mistake.

Saturday morning I set out on the Hollow Ridge loop, a trail I'd done twice before. I was feeling confident, maybe too confident. About forty minutes in, I came to a fork I didn't remember. Both paths looked equally worn. I picked the left one because it seemed to head uphill, which was what I wanted.

Forty minutes later, I was in a thicket with no markers, no switchbacks, and no sign of the ridge. My phone had one bar, then none.

Here's what actually worked. I stopped. I sat down on a log and drank some water, which sounds small but it kept me from panicking and wandering further. Then I used the compass app, which still works offline, to figure out which direction was downhill toward the creek I'd crossed earlier. I followed the creek downstream, since creeks almost always lead to roads or trailheads eventually.

Within an hour I heard a car on a distant road, then spotted a faded blue trail marker on a tree. It was the trail I'd lost.

Lessons learned: carry a paper map, download offline maps before you go, tell someone your route, and when you're lost, stop moving before you do anything else.

Anyone else have a near-miss story? Please share, I'd love to hear them.

**Title: Got lost on the Ridgeline loop yesterday. Found the trail again, barely.**

So I did something dumb yesterday. I took the Ridgeline loop solo, which I've done before, but I figured I didn't need the map because I "knew it." Around the second water crossing I missed the turn where the blue blaze goes left and kept going straight on what I thought was the trail. It was a deer path.

By the time I noticed, the trail was gone. No blazes, just ferns and a lot of downed timber. I had maybe 40% battery on my phone and no signal. Classic.

What actually saved me was hearing the creek. I knew the main trail ran parallel to it on the east side, so I just started walking downhill toward the sound and kept it on my right. It took forever. I fell once and scraped my palm pretty good. At one point I was sure I was going the wrong way and almost turned around, but I kept going.

Eventually I hit a fire road I recognized, which was a huge relief. From there it was twenty minutes to the lot.

Lessons learned: download offline maps, tell someone your route, and don't trust "I know this one" when you're solo. Also, I'm wearing a bandage on my hand at work today and everyone keeps asking.

Anyone else have a "that was stupid but I got out" story from this trail? Curious what other people do when they lose the blazes.

Title: FINALLY DEBT FREE. $14,320 gone. I cried in the grocery store parking lot.

Body:

Long-time lurker, first-time poster. Three years ago I had four credit cards maxed out and a minimum payment list that made me want to hide my phone. Today I made the final payment on the last one, and I'm still kind of stunned.

What worked for me:

**1. I stopped using cards entirely.** I switched to a debit card and cash for everyday spending. This was the hardest part. The first month, I felt like I was missing a limb.

**2. Snowball method.** I listed debts smallest to largest and attacked the smallest one first while paying minimums on the rest. Those early wins kept me going when motivation dipped.

**3. Every raise, every bonus, every tax refund went to debt.** I didn't upgrade my car or my apartment. Mostly I ate a lot of rice and beans.

**4. I called my card companies.** Two of them lowered my interest rates when I asked. It took ten minutes on hold. Ask.

I'm not going to pretend it was fun. But seeing that final "$0.00 balance" was the best feeling I've had in years.

If you're in the middle of it right now, keep going. The math works if you do.

Edit: Thanks for the awards, kind strangers. And yes, I'm celebrating with a very boring cup of coffee.

**Title: Finally got my dashboard to load under 2 seconds, and my manager noticed**

Hey all, not a huge milestone, but it made my week and I want to share it somewhere.

Our internal reporting dashboard has been painfully slow for months. People would click a filter, grab a coffee, and come back to find it still spinning. Everyone just accepted it as "how the tool works."

I finally sat down with the query logs on Monday. Turns out one join was pulling the entire history table on every page load, even when users only needed the last 30 days. I added an index, rewrote the filter so it happened before the join, and cached the summary numbers that don't change often.

Load time went from about 14 seconds to under 2.

Nothing fancy. But on Wednesday, two people from the sales team stopped me in the hallway to say thanks, and one of them said it was the first time the dashboard hadn't made her want to scream. My manager also mentioned it in the team meeting, which I did not expect at all.

Sometimes the small fixes are the ones people actually feel. Anyone else have a quiet win from this week?

**Title: Balcony tomato experiment, week 9. Send help (or tips)**

The peppers, not so much. I bought two jalapeño starters at the hardware store and one of them just sat there looking sad for six weeks before finally deciding to make a single pepper. One. I'm choosing to be proud of it.

The real issue is the lettuce. I planted it in one of those long window boxes and it bolted in like three days during the one heatwave we had. Now it's all tall and bitter and I'm pretty sure I'm just feeding it to the pigeons at this point.

**Title: Got my first rejection from a lit mag today. Weirdly happy about it?**

Posted in r/WritingPrompts (or wherever you lurk)

So I finally did it. Submitted a short story to a small literary magazine back in August, forgot about it, and this morning the form rejection landed in my inbox.

"Thank you for sending us your work. Unfortunately, we will not be publishing this piece."

I expected to feel crushed. Instead I've been grinning at my screen for twenty minutes.

Here's why. For months I've been sending stories into the void, and the silence was worse than any "no." Now I have an actual response from an actual editor. Somebody read it. The story went through a process, and I survived that process.

Some things I'm telling myself:

- Form rejections are not verdicts on talent. Editors reject good stuff all the time because of page budgets, themes, or what else landed that week.
- I now have a tracking spreadsheet, which makes me feel like a professional.
- The magazine's website says they publish "stories that refuse easy answers." Looking at my story again, I think it does that too, so I'm sending it to two more places tonight.

For anyone sitting on their first rejection and dreading it: it's a stamp of participation. Congratulations on being in the game.

What was your first rejection like? Did it sting, or did you celebrate too?

*Edit: Thanks for the kind comments! Yes, I'm aware I'm celebrating a "no." Yes, I'm also aware that I ordered a cheap bottle of champagne.*

**Title: We adopted a 9-year-old lab mix and I'm not sure who's adopting who**

We brought home Biscuit last month. The shelter listed him as "about nine, possibly a little older," gray in the muzzle and a bit stiff in the back legs. Everyone told us to pick a puppy. We didn't want to spend the next decade training a chewed-up couch, so we went with the old guy in the back kennel.

Week one, he slept for about nineteen hours a day. I was sure we'd made a mistake. Week two, he started following me from room to room like a tiny, slow shadow. Week three, he found the one sunny spot on our living room rug and now he's there every afternoon, sighing like he pays the mortgage.

He's not perfect. He snores like a leaf blower, he doesn't do stairs, and he has opinions about the vet's waiting room. But he walks politely on the leash, he doesn't bark at the mail carrier, and he has never once tried to eat a sock. Our vet says he's in good shape for his age, with a few arthritis meds to keep him comfortable.

If you're on the fence about adopting a senior, I'd say do it. The shelter staff said the older dogs are the first to get overlooked, and I get why people skip them. But you get a calm companion who already knows how to be a good dog.

Anyway, Biscuit says hi. Also, he wants me to mention the cheese situation is non-negotiable.

- Minimal cooking equipment (I only have a microwave, a single pan, and a rice cooker)
- Ideas that are fairly healthy, or at least not all carbs

Some things I've tried: lentil soup, bean burritos, and oatmeal with peanut butter. They're fine, but I'm getting bored.

What are your go-to cheap meals? Bonus points for anything you can batch cook on Sunday and eat all week. Recipes, tips for stretching groceries, and store-brand favorites are all welcome. Thanks in advance!

**Title: broke college student here, what are your go-to cheap meals?**

Okay so my meal plan has basically collapsed. Rent went up again and I'm down to about $40 a week for food, and I'm tired of eating plain ramen every night (my roommate has started calling me "the noodle guy").

My kitchen is pretty bare: a rice cooker, a small pot, one pan that's seen better days, and a microwave that works maybe 70% of the time. I can't really do anything that needs an oven.

What I've been doing so far: big batches of rice and lentils, frozen veggies, eggs, and whatever's on sale at the discount grocery. Lentil curry with a bit of curry powder and whatever spinach is left has been the best thing I've made all month, but I'm getting bored.

Stuff I'd love to hear about:
- Meals that stretch for 3+ days, or that freeze well
- Anything that doesn't need much chopping, since my knife is dull
- Ways to make cheap ingredients taste like more than cheap ingredients
- Snacks that aren't just chips

Bonus points if it's vegetarian, but I'm not strict about it. Thanks in advance, I'm gonna be reading every comment.

**I sold my car last March and I've cycled everywhere for a year. Here's the honest verdict.**

Edit: I'm getting a lot of questions, so here are the numbers. I saved roughly $9,400 after insurance, gas, parking, maintenance, and depreciation. That's a lot of concert tickets.

Yes, it rained. A lot. The first winter nearly broke me. Good waterproof gear is not optional, and I wish I'd bought it sooner instead of tough-guying through soaked jeans for three weeks.

The surprises were mostly good. I know my neighborhood in a way I never did from a windshield. I've met three of my neighbors just because we all stop at the same bike rack. My cardio is better than it's been since college, and I've lost about fifteen pounds without trying.

The downsides are real, though. Grocery runs with a backpack and two panniers have a hard limit. Last month I bought a single large bag of dog food and had to walk it home. Trips over 15 miles take planning. And drivers who text while turning are a constant low-level threat that never fully goes away.

Would I do it again? Yes. But I'd tell past me to get a cargo bike sooner, buy better rain gear on day one, and join a local bike group. Ask me anything.

# Salt, Wind, and a Slower Saturday

We left the city before the sun was fully up, the car smelling of coffee and the dashboard still cold. By the time we passed the last gas station, the sky had turned a pale, washed-out blue, and the first gray strip of ocean appeared between the dunes.

We rented a small blue cottage two streets back from the beach. It had creaky floorboards, a kitchen window that wouldn't quite close, and a porch swing that Maya claimed was the best thing about the place. She was right.

Saturday was all about walking. We followed the shoreline for nearly three miles, shoes in hand, letting the cold water chase our ankles. We found a sea glass collection at the tide line: mostly brown and green, with one stubborn piece of cobalt blue that I've decided to keep forever. Gulls argued over a crab shell. A retired fisherman waved at us from his folding chair and told us the water was "colder than it looks, but not as cold as it feels."

That evening we cooked fish tacos badly, laughed about it, and ate them on the porch while the lighthouse beam swept across the water every few seconds.

Sunday was quieter. We drove to a farm stand, bought more peaches than we could possibly eat, and sat in the car with the windows down, not talking much.

Driving home, I kept thinking about how little we actually did. No itinerary, no alarms, just wind, salt, and time that stretched out instead of running away. I think I needed that more than I realized.

I'm already planning the next trip. This time, I'm bringing a better pair of shoes.

# Why I Left My Job to Teach

For eleven years, I was good at my job. I knew the software, the deadlines, and which meetings could have been emails. Nobody complained, and that was part of the problem. I was competent at something I didn't care about, and I could feel the difference every Sunday night.

The moment that changed things was small. A junior colleague asked me to explain a concept I'd used a thousand times. I started to answer, stopped, and realized I wanted to explain it well. I wanted to find the right analogy and watch her face when it clicked. I went home that night and couldn't stop thinking about it.

Quitting was harder than I expected. There was the paycheck, the retirement contributions, and the quiet voice asking whether I was too old to start over. I made a spreadsheet. I talked to people who had made similar changes. I took a part-time evening course in teaching methods just to see if I liked the work when it wasn't an abstraction. I did.

I won't pretend the first semester was easy. I underestimated how much planning goes into one good hour of instruction, and I lost sleep over grading. But something else happened too. On a Tuesday in October, a student who had struggled all term asked a question that showed she had understood something on her own. I had to look at the whiteboard for a moment so no one would see my face.

People ask whether I regret it. I don't. The money is tighter, and some days I miss the predictability of a salary. But I've stopped measuring my days by how little I had to care about them. I now measure them by moments like that one.

If you're sitting with the same restless feeling, I'd say this: you don't have to leap all at once. Take the course, have the conversation, run the numbers. Then decide. The question worth asking isn't whether it's safe, but what you'd regret not trying.

# The Winter I Learned to Bake Bread

The first loaf I baked in January was a brick. I had followed a recipe I found online, measured the flour with more confidence than skill, and pulled out something dense enough to stop a door. My partner ate a slice anyway, out of kindness, and said it was "very sturdy."

I kept going. The cold made it a good excuse. By late afternoon the sun slid behind the neighbors' roofs, the radiator ticked, and the kitchen was the warmest room in the house, so that's where I ended up most evenings.

I learned that flour is never just flour. Humidity changes how much water it wants, and in winter, when the air is dry and the heat is blasting, my dough felt stiff and reluctant. I learned to trust my hands over the recipe's numbers. Dough should feel like an earlobe, my grandmother used to say, and I finally understood what she meant.

I learned patience, too. Bread can't be rushed. The dough needs hours to rise, and the cold stretched those hours longer. I'd set a bowl near the oven, cover it with a towel, and check on it between chores. Some days it doubled. Some days it barely moved, and I had to wait it out.

By February, the loaves were getting better. The crust crackled when it cooled. The crumb had holes, and the bread tasted faintly of wheat and salt and something I can only call patience.

Spring came slowly this year. But I'll remember the winter the kitchen smelled like yeast, the windows fogged up, and every failed loaf taught me something new.

# The Day the Car Died on the M4

It started with a dip on the dashboard, a little amber light shaped like an engine, and I told myself it was nothing. I was doing seventy in the middle lane with a coffee in the cup holder and a podcast I wasn't really listening to. Then the engine note dropped, the speedometer sagged, and the car coughed like it had an opinion about my life choices.

I managed to get onto the hard shoulder before it gave up completely. Cars rushed past, and every gust of wind rocked my little hatchback. I sat there with my hazards ticking and felt absurdly small.

The breakdown service promised forty minutes. It took ninety. I spent the time watching the sky go grey over the fields, eating a stale flapjack from the glovebox, and thinking about how much I rely on machines I don't understand. The recovery driver, a cheerful man named Dev, diagnosed a failed fuel pump in under two minutes and then spent the rest of the trip telling me about his daughter's gymnastics.

I got home late, tired, and oddly grateful. There's something humbling about being stranded. You can't schedule your way out of it. You just wait, and hope someone kind shows up.

The car is in the garage now, costing me more than I'd like. But I keep thinking about that hard shoulder, the strangers slowing to check on me, and the small mercy of a stranger's voice on the phone saying, "Right, let's have a look."

# What My Failed Side Project Taught Me

Last spring I spent four months building a habit tracker for houseplants. It would remind you to water, log soil moisture, and show a little graph of each plant's health. I designed the logo, wrote the onboarding flow, and set up a landing page with a waitlist. The waitlist got eleven signups, and seven of them were my friends.

I shut it down in August without much ceremony.

Looking back, the problem wasn't the code. The code was fine. The problem was that I built what seemed interesting to build instead of what anyone had asked for. I never talked to a single person who owned a struggling fern. I assumed my own forgetfulness represented a market.

I also learned that I'd been using the project to avoid something else. Every time my job felt stuck, I'd open the repository and feel productive. Polishing a settings page felt like progress, even when nothing I shipped was reaching anyone. Side projects can become a comfortable place to hide.

A few things I'd tell my past self:

- **Talk to users before writing code.** Five conversations would have saved me three months.
- **Set a small, testable goal early.** "Will ten strangers pay for this?" is a better question than "Is the architecture clean?"
- **Notice when you're avoiding something.** Ask whether the project is the thing you want or just the thing that feels safe.

The plants, for the record, are doing fine. My neighbor took over my pothos, and it's thriving. Apparently, it never needed an app. It needed someone to remember to water it, and that turned out to be a much simpler problem.

# The Books That Carried My Summer

Summer always gets away from me, and this year was no different. Somewhere between the long evenings and the lazy weekend mornings, I found myself with a stack of books I didn't quite plan to read, and I'm glad I did.

I started with [first book title], which I picked up on a whim at the library. I expected a light beach read, but it surprised me with its quiet honesty. I read the last third in one sitting on my porch while the sun went down.

Next came [second book title], a book my sister had been urging on me for months. I resisted for a while, mostly out of stubbornness, but once I started, I couldn't put it down. Its characters stayed with me long after I finished, and I caught myself thinking about them during my morning walks.

Midsummer, I wandered into [third book title] almost by accident. It's the kind of book that asks you to slow down and pay attention, and I'm grateful it made me do that. I underlined more passages in it than in any other book this year.

Looking back, what I valued most wasn't any single story but the rhythm reading gave my days. Some evenings I read for an hour, other times for ten minutes before bed, but the habit kept me company through the heat and the busy stretches.

If you've been meaning to read more, let this be your nudge. Keep a book on the kitchen table or in your bag. You might be surprised by what finds you.

What did you read this summer? I'd love your recommendations for the months ahead.

Summer got away from me. I meant to read a stack of books on the porch, and I ended up reading about three and a half of them, mostly in the car at the lake while the kids were in the water.

I started with *Piranesi* because a friend kept pushing it on me. I finished it in two sittings. The house with all its endless halls got under my skin, and I kept thinking about it while I was doing dishes. I'm still not sure I understood the ending, but I didn't mind.

Then I tried *The Overstory*, which was a mistake. Not because it's bad. It's just long, and I kept putting it down to check my phone. I did finish it, though, and the chapter about the trees made me go outside and look at the big oak in our yard like I'd never seen it before. Kind of embarrassing, honestly.

The best one was *Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow*. My sister gave it to me in June and I almost didn't start it because the cover looked like every other book on the bestseller table. I read the whole thing on a rainy Sunday and then texted her at eleven at night asking why she hadn't told me it would wreck me.

The half-finished one is a history of the Erie Canal that I got about a third of the way through before I lost interest. I'll probably go back to it in January, when I've got nothing better to do.

Anyway, that's the summer. Next year I'm bringing a bigger bag.

# Learning to Be Someone's Father

Nobody warned me about the silence. Not the crying, which I expected, but the quiet moments at 3 a.m. when I'd stand over the crib and listen to my daughter breathe, certain that if I looked away for even a second, something would go wrong.

I used to think I understood responsibility. I had a job, a mortgage, a dog who depended on me for dinner. But none of that prepared me for a person who would depend on me completely, who couldn't tell me what hurt or what she wanted, and who would eventually grow into someone with opinions of her own.

The first weeks blurred together. Bottles, diapers, the strange math of sleep in two-hour pieces. My partner and I became a small, exhausted team, passing the baby back and forth like a relay baton. Some nights we argued over nothing. Some nights we just held each other on the couch and laughed at how little we knew.

What surprised me most was how quickly the fear turned into something else. Not confidence, exactly. More like a steady willingness to keep showing up. I learned to read her cries the way you learn a new language, one word at a time. I started narrating my day to her, even the boring parts, because she seemed to like the sound of my voice.

People tell you parenthood changes you. It does, but not in a single dramatic moment. It happens in small, ordinary repetitions: the bath, the lullaby I sing off-key, the tiny hand that grabs my finger and won't let go.

I don't have it figured out. I probably never will. But I'm learning that showing up, again and again, is most of the job.

The Month I Tried to Spend Nothing

I made it four days before my first purchase. It was a carton of oat milk, and I felt almost relieved buying it.

The rules I set for myself were simple. No money out for thirty days. Rent, utilities, and the phone bill were exempt, since those were already scheduled and I couldn't exactly skip them. Everything else was off limits: coffee, takeout, that impulse browse through the bookstore, the streaming subscription I forgot I had.

The first week was almost fun. I cooked from the pantry, found a forgotten bag of lentils, and felt like a contestant on a cooking show with a strict budget. I walked to places I'd normally drive. I started noticing how often my hand drifted toward my wallet out of habit alone.

By week two, the novelty had worn off. Friends invited me out, and I either had to explain my experiment or make up excuses. I learned that spending is rarely just about the thing you buy. It's about connection, comfort, and small rewards after a long day. Saying no to a drink felt like saying no to people.

The hardest moment came on day nineteen, after a bad meeting. I wanted a treat so badly that I stood in the grocery aisle holding a candy bar for five minutes, debating. I put it back. Then I felt ridiculous for how much that mattered.

By the end, I had saved a little over two hundred dollars, which is nice but not the real story. What changed was my awareness. I now know exactly how much of my spending was automatic, and how much of it I could live without.

I didn't spend nothing. But I spent a lot more thoughtfully, and that might be the more useful result.

# Still Sharing the Fridge at Thirty-Four

Last week I found a container of rice in the back of the fridge with a label that said "DO NOT TOUCH - Dana." Dana moved out in the spring. The rice is older than some of my houseplants.

I thought I'd be out of shared housing by now. In my twenties, roommates made sense: cheap rent, a warm body in the next room, someone to split the internet bill. Somewhere along the way, I assumed I'd graduate to a place with my name on the lease and a dishwasher I didn't have to negotiate over.

Instead, I'm here. My roommate Priya and I have a system. We alternate Sunday grocery runs, we've agreed the thermostat stays at 68, and we have a shared spreadsheet that tracks who owes whom for toilet paper. It's not glamorous, but it works.

What surprised me is how much I've come to like it. At thirty-four, I'm not chasing the nightly party or the couch-surfing adventure. I want someone to ask how my day went, someone to split a bottle of wine with on a Tuesday, and someone who will notice when I've been quiet for too long. Priya has done all three.

Living with roommates in your thirties isn't a failure to launch. Rent is high, and most of us aren't on a path that looks like the one our parents followed. Sharing a home is a practical choice, and sometimes it's a generous one.

Still, I'm starting a new label-maker fund. The rice has to go. Priya agrees. We've scheduled a meeting about it.

# Goodbye, Coffee (For Now)

For eleven years, my mornings started the same way: the grinder's whine, the hiss of the kettle, that first bitter sip before my feet even found the floor. Coffee wasn't just a drink. It was a ritual, a reason to get up, and honestly, a bit of an identity.

So when my doctor mentioned my restless nights and racing heart, I didn't argue. I just went quiet and started thinking about what I'd lose.

The first week was rough. I got headaches that pulsed behind my eyes, and I snapped at my partner over nothing. I kept walking to the kitchen out of habit, staring at the empty spot where the French press used to sit. I tried herbal tea, and it tasted like warm hay.

Then something shifted. Around day ten, I woke up before my alarm without feeling like I'd been hit by a truck. My afternoons stopped crashing into a fog. I noticed the smell of rain through the open window and the way the neighbor's dog trots when it's happy.

I haven't become a tea evangelist. I still miss the cafe on the corner, the easy conversation over a flat white, the small theater of ordering. Some mornings I stand in the kitchen and feel a little foolish, waiting for a caffeine kick that won't come.

But I'm sleeping better, and my heart has settled. Coffee and I may reunite someday, maybe in moderation, maybe on weekends. For now, I'm learning that a morning can be good without it.

If you're thinking about cutting back, talk to your doctor first. And if you're in the middle of those headache days, hang in there. It gets quieter.

# Why We Should Go Back to Venus

Venus is often called Earth's twin. It is similar in size, mass, and composition, yet it is a scorching world where surface temperatures reach about 465°C (870°F), hot enough to melt lead. Some people argue that such a hostile planet is not worth the cost of exploration. I disagree. Venus deserves renewed attention because it can teach us about planetary science, help us understand our own climate, and inspire the next generation of engineers.

First, Venus offers a natural laboratory for studying how planets evolve. Scientists still do not fully understand why Venus and Earth, which formed from similar material, developed so differently. Learning what drove Venus toward a runaway greenhouse effect could sharpen our models of how climate systems can tip out of balance. Understanding that process is not an abstract exercise. It bears directly on the future of our own planet.

Second, exploration of Venus pushes technology forward. Its surface pressure is about 90 times that of Earth's, and its acidic clouds make it difficult to observe. Engineers who design probes capable of surviving these conditions develop materials, cooling systems, and communication methods that can be used in other fields, from deep-sea research to nuclear energy. Each mission to a difficult environment expands what humans can build.

Critics point out that Venus is expensive and dangerous to reach, and that the money could go to problems on Earth. That concern is serious, but it misses an important point. Space science has consistently produced benefits far beyond its original goals, and investment in planetary missions also supports jobs, education, and international cooperation. Robotic missions are relatively affordable compared with human spaceflight, and they can operate for years, gathering data that no single generation could collect alone.

Finally, Venus invites curiosity. Humans have always been drawn to the unknown, and our sister planet is full of questions. Why does it rotate backward? Could its upper atmosphere ever have hosted life? Answering these questions requires patient, sustained exploration.

Venus is harsh, but that is precisely why it matters. We should explore it, learn from it, and let it teach us about the fragile world we call home.

# The Facial Action Coding System Is a Valuable Research Tool, but Not a Lie Detector

The Facial Action Coding System (FACS), developed by Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen in 1978, breaks facial movement into discrete components called Action Units. Each unit corresponds to a specific muscle movement, such as raising the inner brow or tightening the lips. Trained coders can use FACS to describe any facial expression objectively, without assuming what the person feels. This precision makes FACS one of the most useful tools in psychology, and its value should not be questioned. Its misuse, however, should be.

FACS is an excellent instrument for describing what faces do. Researchers use it to study infant development, track pain in patients who cannot speak, and analyze the subtle timing of expressions in conversation. Because the system records movement rather than meaning, it avoids the bias of a coder deciding in advance what a face "must" mean. This descriptive neutrality is its greatest strength.

The problem begins when FACS descriptions are treated as evidence of emotion. Ekman's original work argued that certain expressions were universal, but later research has complicated that claim. A 2019 review by Barrett and colleagues found that facial movements vary considerably across cultures, situations, and individuals, and that a single movement, such as a smile or frown, does not reliably indicate one emotion. Yet commercial products now claim to read employees' feelings during job interviews or detect deception at border checkpoints using automated facial analysis.

These applications are dangerous. A system that misreads nervousness as dishonesty can unfairly deny someone a job or subject them to suspicion. Because the people affected rarely understand how these judgments are made, they have little power to contest them.

FACS should remain a rigorous method for studying facial behavior, used by researchers who understand its limits. It should not serve as a shortcut to judging character or truthfulness. Scientific humility requires recognizing that a face shows what muscles are doing, not necessarily what a person is thinking or feeling.

Driverless Cars Should Be Embraced

Every year, traffic accidents kill more than 1.2 million people worldwide, and the overwhelming majority of these crashes are caused by human error. Drivers get distracted by phones, drive while intoxicated, fall asleep at the wheel, and misjudge speed and distance. Driverless cars offer a way to remove these everyday failures from the road, and for that reason they should be embraced rather than feared.

The most important argument for autonomous vehicles is safety. Self-driving systems do not text, tire, or become impaired by alcohol. They scan their surroundings continuously in every direction, reacting in fractions of a second. Although the technology is still improving and has faced well-publicized failures, the long-term data points toward a substantial reduction in crashes once these vehicles are widely deployed. Saving even a fraction of those 1.2 million lives would justify the investment.

Driverless cars also promise greater independence and opportunity. Millions of people, including the elderly, people with disabilities, and those who cannot afford a car with a licensed driver, currently struggle to travel freely. Autonomous vehicles could give them reliable access to jobs, medical appointments, and social life. In this way, the technology is not only about convenience but also about fairness and inclusion.

Critics raise valid concerns about job losses for professional drivers, cybersecurity risks, and unclear liability when a computer makes a fatal mistake. These concerns deserve serious answers, such as retraining programs, strict security standards, and clear legal frameworks that assign responsibility to manufacturers and operators. Problems to be solved, however, are not reasons to reject a technology that could prevent tragedy on a massive scale.

Some people argue that they simply enjoy driving and do not want to surrender control. That preference is understandable, but it cannot outweigh the lives at stake on public roads. Society already accepts many rules that limit personal freedom for collective safety, such as seatbelt laws and speed limits.

Driverless cars are not perfect, but they are far safer than the human drivers they are meant to replace. Governments and companies should support their development, testing, and responsible deployment. The question is not whether we can afford to adopt this technology, but whether we can afford to keep waiting while preventable deaths continue on our roads.

Driverless cars should be allowed on public roads, and the case for them is stronger than most people think. The biggest reason is safety. Human drivers cause over 90 percent of serious crashes, usually because they are distracted, tired, or drinking. A computer doesn't text on the highway or check its phone at a red light. Even though self-driving systems still make mistakes, they don't get bored or angry, and they can watch every direction at once.

Critics often say that driverless cars are not ready, and they point to accidents that have happened during testing. Those accidents deserve attention, but they shouldn't be the whole story. Every new technology has a rough start. Planes crashed in the early days of aviation, and nobody suggested we ban flying. What matters is whether the technology gets better over time and whether it ends up saving more lives than it costs. Human driving has been killing about 40,000 Americans a year for decades, so the bar is not perfection. The bar is beating what we already have.

Another argument is access. Right now, people who are elderly, disabled, or simply unable to drive have a hard time getting around. A driverless car could take a grandmother to the doctor or a blind man to work without anyone needing to ask a friend for a ride. That kind of independence matters a lot, and it's something gas-powered cars never gave to everyone.

Some people worry about jobs, especially truck drivers and taxi drivers. That concern is real and deserves real help, like retraining programs and time to adjust. But stopping safer technology to protect one job category isn't a fair trade for everyone else who would benefit.

Driverless cars are not perfect yet, and the rules should be strict. But the goal should be to make them work well and then let them spread, not to keep them off the road because people feel nervous about giving up the wheel. The data suggests the machines will eventually be the safer drivers, and when that happens, we should be ready to let them drive.

Cell Phones Should Be Banned During School Hours

Cell phones have become almost constant companions, but school is the one place where their presence does more harm than good. Schools exist to help students focus, learn, and build social skills. Phones work against each of these goals, which is why cell phones should be banned during the school day.

The most obvious problem is distraction. A phone on a desk invites constant checking, whether for a text, a notification, or a quick look at social media. Research on attention suggests that even the mere presence of a phone can reduce concentration and working memory, because part of the brain stays busy resisting the urge to check it. Students who are trying to understand a math proof or analyze a poem cannot afford that divided attention.

Phones also undermine the social life of the school. Lunch periods and hallways should be spaces for conversation, friendship, and conflict resolution. When students spend these moments scrolling, they miss chances to practice face-to-face communication, which is a skill they will need in college and in every job they ever hold. Cyberbullying and the spread of embarrassing photos are further problems that a phone-free day can reduce.

Opponents argue that phones are essential for emergencies and for learning tools. Those concerns deserve respect, but they do not justify unrestricted use. Schools already have phones in every office, and parents can reach the front desk in an emergency. Educational apps and laptops can be used under teacher supervision when a lesson requires them. A ban on personal phones does not remove technology from the classroom; it simply ensures that technology serves the lesson rather than competing with it.

Some students fear that a ban will be hard to enforce. Many schools have already shown otherwise. Phone-free policies, such as storing devices in lockers or pouches during class, have reduced distractions and improved focus in many districts. Clear rules, consistent consequences, and parental cooperation make these policies workable.

School should be the place where students learn to think deeply and connect with one another. Keeping cell phones out of the school day gives them the space to do both. For the sake of attention, friendship, and learning, schools should ban cell phones during class time and the full school day.

**Distance Learning Cannot Replace the Classroom**

Distance learning promised to make education more accessible. Students could learn from home, attend lessons across the country, and study at their own pace. Yet the experience of recent years shows that online instruction, however convenient, cannot replace the classroom. Schools should use distance learning as a supplement, not a substitute, for in-person education.

The most serious problem with distance learning is the loss of human connection. Learning depends on relationships. A teacher who notices a student's confusion during a lesson, or who offers encouragement after a struggle, provides guidance that no screen can fully replicate. Students also learn social skills, such as cooperation, conflict resolution, and empathy, through daily interaction with peers. When these experiences disappear behind a webcam, students often become isolated, and many fall behind academically and emotionally.

Distance learning also deepens existing inequalities. Not every household has reliable internet, a quiet place to study, or a parent available to help with schoolwork. Students who lack these resources are the ones most harmed when schools move online. Classrooms, by contrast, offer a level playing field, with equipment, supervision, and support available to all students regardless of their home circumstances.

Critics respond that distance learning offers flexibility for students with jobs, illnesses, or long commutes. This is a fair point, and it explains why online options should remain available. A hybrid approach, in which students attend in person for core instruction and use online tools for review or specialized courses, captures these benefits without sacrificing the advantages of the classroom.

Finally, the purpose of education extends beyond the transfer of information. Schools prepare young people to live and work among others. Remote screens cannot teach the discipline of showing up, the give-and-take of a group discussion, or the experience of belonging to a community.

Distance learning has a legitimate place in modern education, but it should remain a tool that supports the classroom rather than replaces it. Schools that prioritize in-person learning while offering flexible online options will best serve their students.

Seeking Multiple Opinions

Most people have a favorite source they trust. Maybe it's a parent, a best friend, a teacher, or the first article that popped up on their phone. It feels efficient to settle on one voice and let it do the thinking. But relying on a single opinion is a mistake, and people should actively seek out several perspectives before they form a view on anything important.

The first reason is simple: no single person knows everything. Even experts are limited by their training, their experiences, and the circles they move in. A doctor who specializes in one area may not see the bigger picture. A politician listens mostly to the people who vote for them. When you hear from only one source, you inherit its blind spots without ever knowing they exist. Comparing a few viewpoints is the only reliable way to spot what one of them left out.

Second, hearing different opinions makes your own thinking sharper. When you have to explain why one argument is stronger than another, you start to understand the issue instead of just repeating what you were told. Disagreement forces you to check your assumptions. Sometimes you discover your original view was wrong. Other times you find that it holds up, and now you can defend it with real reasons instead of habit.

Some people argue that seeking many opinions leads to confusion or indecision. If everyone has a different take, how do you ever choose? That concern is fair, but it misses the point. The goal is not to agree with everyone. The goal is to gather enough information to make a decision you can stand behind. Weighing several views takes more effort than following one, but that effort is what separates a considered judgment from a guess.

Finally, seeking multiple opinions is a matter of respect. It treats other people as thinkers worth listening to, not just obstacles to be argued down. It also keeps us humble. Nobody enjoys finding out they were confidently wrong, but it happens to everyone, and the people who ask around tend to find out sooner.

So the next time you face a big question, resist the urge to pick the first answer you hear. Ask a friend who disagrees with you. Read something from the other side. Your conclusion may end up the same, but it will be better for having been tested.

**The Cowboy Who Rode the Waves: Courage Is Not Bound to a Place**

A cowboy belongs on the range, or so tradition insists. He knows horses, dust, and open plains, and the saddle is his natural seat. Yet the image of a cowboy who rides the waves challenges that assumption, and it argues convincingly that a person's courage and skill matter more than the landscape they were born into. The cowboy who learns to ride the sea is not a contradiction. He is proof that identity is built through action, not inherited from geography.

The strongest argument for this view is that the core skills of the cowboy are not really about land. Balance, patience, reading a living creature's moods, and staying calm under sudden motion are useful everywhere. A rider who can stay upright on a bucking horse already understands how to move with an unpredictable force. Moving that understanding from grassland to ocean requires humility and practice, but it does not require abandoning who he is. The waves demand the same qualities that the range did.

Critics might argue that the cowboy is simply out of place, and that trying to be something new dilutes tradition. This objection misunderstands what traditions are. Every tradition began when someone first did something unexpected. The cowboy culture itself grew from people adapting Spanish horsemanship to new land and new needs. A tradition that refuses to adapt is not preserved; it is merely frozen. Honoring the cowboy means honoring his willingness to meet a challenge, even one far from home.

Finally, the cowboy who rides the waves reminds us that fear of the unfamiliar keeps people small. Many of us assume we are only capable of what we have always done. The waves represent the unknown, and choosing to face them expresses a kind of freedom the open range never fully offered. Courage, after all, is most meaningful when it is tested somewhere new.

In the end, the cowboy's story suggests that we should judge people by what they dare and how they grow, not by the boundaries they were given. A rider is defined by his willingness to stay in the saddle, whether the ground beneath him is dry earth or moving water.

Should Students Be Required to Complete a Year of Community Service Before Graduating?

Requiring a year of community service before graduation would give students experiences that classrooms cannot. Service work teaches responsibility, exposes young people to problems beyond their own neighborhoods, and builds the habit of contributing to a community. For these reasons, the requirement deserves serious consideration.

The strongest argument for the requirement is that it broadens students' perspectives. A teenager who has spent months tutoring children, staffing a food bank, or caring for elderly residents begins to understand how other people live. Such understanding is difficult to gain from textbooks alone, and it can reduce the isolation and indifference that often come with a narrow social world.

Critics argue that mandatory service undermines its own purpose. Volunteering is meaningful because it is freely chosen, and forced labor may breed resentment rather than compassion. Some students also already work part-time jobs or care for family members, and an additional year of required service could add pressure to an already full schedule. Schools might also struggle to find enough meaningful placements, leaving students with busywork that teaches little.

These concerns are real, but they can be addressed through thoughtful design. A requirement could offer flexible options, such as service through religious groups, local organizations, or family caregiving, and it could count hours toward a total rather than demanding a single uninterrupted year. Schools could also reflect with students on what they learned, turning service into an education rather than a checkbox.

Ultimately, a graduation requirement signals what a society values. A year of service would tell students that their education is meant to prepare them not only for careers but for citizenship. If designed with flexibility and care, it would be a worthwhile step toward graduates who understand and serve the communities they will join.
