items.family: persuade:A Cowboy Who Rode the Waves
items.text:
Some readers dismiss the image of a cowboy riding waves as a silly mismatch, a Western hero dropped into an ocean he was never meant to cross. That reaction misses the point. A cowboy who rides the waves shows that skill is portable, and that a person's character can carry them into unfamiliar territory.

The cowboy's central asset is not the horse or the saddle. It is patience, balance, and a steady read of the animal beneath him. Those qualities do not disappear when the ground turns to water. A rider who has spent years watching a horse's shifting weight knows how to anticipate motion, stay loose in the hips, and keep calm when the world tilts. The waves demand the same attention. The story suggests that expertise is less about a specific place than about the habits a person builds while learning to respect something larger than himself.

Critics might argue that the premise is implausible, and they are right that no one would literally mistake a saddle for a surfboard. But fiction does not need to be literal to be meaningful. The absurdity is the invitation. By placing a figure of the open range on the open sea, the story asks readers to imagine how their own experience might transfer to places they have never been. A student who has mastered one subject, or a worker who has changed careers, is in the same position as this cowboy. Adaptation is not a betrayal of one's roots. It is proof that those roots were strong enough to grow new branches.

There is also a lesson about humility. The cowboy does not conquer the ocean. He rides it, moving with its rhythm rather than fighting it. That posture is valuable in any setting where a person is a beginner, and it reminds us that competence in one domain should lead to curiosity in another, not arrogance.

For these reasons, the image of a cowboy riding the waves deserves more than a smile. It argues that character travels, that imagination thrives on unlikely pairings, and that the best way to meet an unfamiliar world is to bring what we have learned and remain willing to be humbled by the new one.

Should Students Be Required to Do Community Service Before Graduating?

I think high school students should be required to do a year of community service before they graduate. Some people say it is unfair to make students work for free, but I think the benefits are bigger than the complaints.

First, community service teaches things you cannot learn from a textbook. When you volunteer at a food bank or help out at an elderly home, you actually see how people live. Last summer I helped at a animal shelter and I met a lady who had lost her job and was trying to feed her kids. I never would have understood that from a book. I think every student should have experiences like that before they go out into the world.

Second, a lot of kids today spend all their time on their phones and don't really talk to people outside their friend group. Community service makes you work with different kinds of people, including adults and people from different backgrounds. That skill is useful for jobs and for life in general.

Some students say they already have too much homework and extracurriculars, and they don't have time for another requirement. That is a fair point. But a year is not that much time, and the schools could make it flexible, like letting students do service on weekends or during summer break. Also, many colleges already look for volunteer work on applications, so students who are forced to do it early might find they enjoy it and keep going.

Finally, requiring service sends a message that we are all part of a community and we should help each other. I think that is a lesson worth teaching in school.

So yes, I think students should be required to do a year of community service. It helps them grow, it builds skills, and it helps the people around them.

Should Schools Have a Four-Day Week?

The traditional five-day school week has long been treated as a fixed rule of education, but a growing number of districts have questioned whether it serves students best. A four-day week, with longer daily lessons and a three-day weekend, deserves serious consideration. It can improve attendance, help teachers, and save money, though it must be carefully designed to protect learning.

The strongest argument for a four-day week is attendance. Students in rural districts, where families may travel long distances, often miss school for appointments, errands, and family responsibilities. A shorter week reduces the number of days that can be lost, and some districts that adopted it have reported fewer absences. Teachers also benefit. Extra time away from the classroom can reduce burnout and make it easier to attract and keep qualified staff, especially in areas where pay is low.

Financial savings are another reason districts consider the change. Fewer operating days mean lower costs for utilities, transportation, and food service. Those savings can be redirected toward tutoring or higher salaries.

Critics, however, raise legitimate concerns. Longer school days can tire younger students, and working families may struggle to find childcare on the fifth day off. Some studies have found small drops in achievement in certain subjects, and there is a risk that students from low-income households, who may rely on school meals and supervision, will lose out most.

Ultimately, the answer depends on implementation. A four-day week should not simply cut time from the calendar. Schools should ensure lessons remain rigorous, provide support for children who need it, and plan for childcare. Done thoughtfully, a four-day week can be a practical way to help both students and teachers succeed.

Learning from our own mistakes is valuable, but it is not always the most efficient path. The best learning often comes from combining personal experience with the wisdom of others.

Mistakes teach lessons that stay with us. When we touch a hot stove, we never forget it. Errors we make ourselves carry emotional weight, forcing us to reflect on what went wrong and why. This reflection builds judgment, which cannot be fully handed down through instruction. A student who fails a test after poor preparation often changes study habits for good, because the consequence was real and personal.

However, learning only from our own mistakes has serious limits. Some errors are too costly to make even once. A surgeon cannot afford to learn every technique through trial and error, and a driver who ignores others' warnings about icy roads may cause an accident. Other people have already walked many of the paths we are considering. Their advice condenses years of experience into a few sentences, saving us time and pain. Teachers, parents, and mentors often see patterns that we, focused on our own situations, cannot.

Advice has its own weakness, though. Words alone rarely feel as convincing as experience. We may nod along to a friend's warning about a bad investment, then repeat the same mistake because we did not truly believe it until we felt the loss ourselves. Advice becomes powerful only when we are willing to listen, consider it seriously, and test it against our circumstances.

The wisest approach blends both sources. We should use others' advice to avoid obvious dangers and to gain perspective, while reserving our own mistakes as opportunities for deeper growth. Those who learn only from themselves may repeat avoidable harm, and those who learn only from others may never develop independent judgment. Ultimately, the strongest learners are those who treat advice as a guide and their own errors as honest teachers.

Should students get to pick their own classes? I used to think the answer was obviously yes. Then I spent a semester in a class I picked because the schedule fit, and I learned that choosing something and wanting it are different things.

Still, I think students should have a real say. Nobody knows a student's life better than the student. A kid who works nights at a grocery store, or who is already thinking about becoming a nurse, has information that a counselor with two hundred advisees does not. When students pick classes, they tend to show up. They ask questions. They do the reading because they chose the topic, even when it's dull.

The problem is that choice can slide into avoidance. Plenty of kids would happily skip anything with math in it, or take the easiest history elective with the friendliest teacher. Left completely alone, many students would build a schedule that feels good now and leaves them underprepared later. That's where adults come in. Schools can require a core of subjects everyone needs, like reading, writing, and basic math, and then let students fill the remaining slots with what they actually care about.

There's also a question of what school is for. If it's only about job training, then letting kids choose is risky, because they can't predict what they'll need. If school is also about becoming a person who can think about things you didn't expect to care about, then some choices should stretch you. Some of my best classes were ones I almost didn't sign up for.

So yes, students should choose, but within limits. Give them real options, honest advice, and a required foundation. Let them own the rest, including the mistakes.

Should Young People Start Working Part-Time Jobs in High School?

Many students today face a choice that previous generations rarely had to consider: whether to take on a part-time job while still in high school. Some argue that teenagers should focus entirely on their studies and activities, while others believe that early work experience builds essential skills. Young people should start working part-time jobs in high school, as long as they keep their academic performance a priority.

The most obvious benefit of a part-time job is financial independence. Teenagers who earn their own money learn to budget, save, and make spending decisions. They may pay for their own clothes, phone bills, or entertainment, which relieves some pressure on their families. These lessons in money management often prove more valuable than anything taught in a classroom.

Work also teaches responsibility and time management. A student who must arrive on time for a shift, meet the expectations of a manager, and still finish homework learns to plan carefully. Employers offer something that school often cannot: real consequences. Missing a shift affects coworkers, and doing good work earns trust and future opportunities. These experiences prepare young people for college and careers.

Critics worry that jobs take time away from studying and sleep. This concern is valid, and it is why students should limit their hours, perhaps to fifteen or twenty per week. When balanced properly, a job can actually sharpen focus, since students with limited time often use it more efficiently. Many also gain a sense of purpose and confidence from being useful outside the home.

In conclusion, a part-time job during high school can teach financial responsibility, discipline, and real-world skills. Students should work, but they should never let work replace their education.

Technology and the Question of Connection

Technology has changed how people connect, but it has not simply made them less social. Instead, it has reshaped the way social life happens. A century ago, friendships often depended on living nearby, and communication meant letters that took weeks to arrive. Today, a person can video chat with a relative overseas or join a community of strangers who share a hobby. These tools have made it easier to maintain distant relationships and to find people who understand us.

Critics argue, however, that screens pull attention away from face-to-face contact. Families sit together at dinner while each person scrolls through a phone, and friends meet in person but spend the evening checking messages. Research on teenagers has suggested that heavy social media use is linked to feelings of loneliness, though the findings are far from conclusive. The concern is less that technology removes people from one another and more that it can replace deeper conversation with quick, shallow exchanges.

The real answer depends on how technology is used. A video call that lets a grandparent watch a grandchild grow up is deeply social. A late-night feed that keeps someone isolated in their room is not. The difference lies in whether technology supports real relationships or substitutes for them.

Ultimately, technology is a tool, and like any tool, its effects depend on the hand that holds it. It can widen our circles or narrow them. If people treat their devices as bridges to one another rather than walls between them, technology can make society richer. The challenge for each person is to decide which path to take.

Should School Start Later in the Morning?

Many American high schools start before 8:00 a.m., yet teenagers' bodies are biologically wired to sleep later. During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts so that teens naturally feel alert at night and drowsy in the early morning. Because of this change, a later start time would likely help students learn, stay healthy, and succeed.

Sleep is essential for memory and concentration. Teenagers who get too little rest struggle to focus, retain information, and perform well on tests. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that adolescents get between eight and ten hours of sleep each night, but most fall short. An early bell forces many students to wake before their bodies are ready, so they begin each day already tired. A later start would give them the chance to meet their sleep needs.

Health is also at stake. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to depression, anxiety, obesity, and weakened immune systems. Students who are rushed out of bed may also skip breakfast or rely on caffeine and energy drinks to get through the day. Later start times could support both physical and emotional well-being.

Critics argue that later schedules would create problems for working parents, sports practices, and bus routes. These concerns are real, and districts that have changed their schedules have had to plan carefully. However, many schools that adopted later start times reported improved attendance and fewer tardies, suggesting that the benefits can outweigh the difficulties when schedules are managed thoughtfully.

Ultimately, schools exist to help students learn and grow. If starting later allows young people to be rested, healthy, and ready to learn, then it is a change worth making.

Is It Important to Have a Positive Attitude?

A positive attitude is often dismissed as wishful thinking, yet it remains one of the most valuable tools a person can carry. It is important not because it guarantees success or erases hardship, but because it shapes how we respond to the difficulties that inevitably arise.

Consider two students who fail a difficult exam. The first sees the result as proof of inability and stops trying. The second treats the failure as information, identifies weak areas, and studies differently the next time. Both faced the same setback, but their attitudes determined what came next. A positive outlook does not deny the disappointment; it directs attention toward what can still be changed.

Attitude also affects the people around us. Optimism and encouragement are contagious. A teammate who believes the group can recover from a losing streak often motivates others to keep playing with energy. Conversely, constant negativity can drain morale and make cooperation harder. In school, at work, and in friendships, a hopeful disposition makes others more willing to collaborate and take risks.

Health may be affected as well. Research on stress and optimism suggests that people who expect favorable outcomes often cope with pressure more effectively, which can support both mental and physical well-being. While the relationship is complex, it is clear that persistent anxiety and cynicism take a toll.

However, a positive attitude must be genuine and grounded in reality. Forced cheerfulness that ignores real problems can be as unhelpful as despair. The healthiest form of optimism acknowledges difficulty honestly while maintaining confidence in one's capacity to respond.

In the end, a positive attitude matters because it turns obstacles into opportunities for growth. It does not promise an easy path, but it makes the journey more bearable and more likely to lead somewhere worthwhile. For that reason, it is indeed important.

Should Students Be Allowed to Take Classes Online From Home?

In my opinion, students should be allowed to take classes online from home, because it give them more flexibility and freedom. Many students have part-time jobs or need to take care of family members, so attending school in person every day is very difficult for them. With online classes, they can study at their own pace and manage their time better. They can also save money on transportation and sometimes on housing, which is important for families with low income.

Another reason is that online learning allow students to access courses that are not available in their local area. For example, a student in a small village may not have a university nearby that teaches the subject they want. Through the internet, they can join a class from any top school in the world. This make education more fair and open for everyone.

Some people argue that students at home are easy to distract, and they do not have the same support from teachers and friends. This is true for some students, especially young children or those who lack self-discipline. However, these problems can be reduced with good planning, regular video meetings, and clear rules from schools. Teachers can also check students' progress more often to make sure no one falls behind.

In conclusion, I believe online classes from home should be allowed. They help students balance their lives, reach more opportunities, and learn in a way that suits them. Of course, schools should make sure that students still get enough interaction and guidance. With the right support, online learning can be a very useful choice for many students.

**The Right Time to Begin**

There is no single best age to start a career, but the most rewarding time to begin is usually in the early-to-mid twenties. By then, most people have finished a foundational education, gained some independence, and developed enough maturity to make deliberate choices, yet they still have decades ahead to adjust course.

Starting early has clear advantages. Young workers often have more flexibility to relocate, take risks, and try unfamiliar roles. Mistakes made at twenty-two cost less than those made at forty-five, with fewer mortgages, dependents, or established reputations to protect. Early experience also compounds: a person who begins working in their late teens or early twenties accumulates skills, professional networks, and retirement savings that grow over time.

However, rushing into a career can carry its own costs. Someone who commits too quickly, without exploring their interests, may find themselves stuck in work that offers little satisfaction. Many people benefit from taking time to study, travel, volunteer, or hold jobs in several fields before settling on a path. The stories of successful people who changed careers in their thirties, forties, or later show that late starts are not failures. Experience gained elsewhere often becomes an asset in a new field.

The best age, then, depends on the person. A nurse or engineer may need to begin training immediately, while a writer or entrepreneur might gain valuable perspective by working in other industries first. What matters most is not the number of years but the quality of reflection behind the decision.

In the end, the ideal moment to start a career is when a person has enough self-knowledge to choose wisely and enough courage to begin. For most, that moment arrives in their early twenties, but the path is rarely straight, and that is part of its value.

The Value of Boredom

We have engineered boredom out of our lives almost entirely. Waiting in line, riding the elevator, sitting at a red light: each of these gaps once held nothing but our own thoughts, and now a phone fills them before they can open. We reach for screens the way a tongue finds a missing tooth, reflexively and without quite deciding to. Boredom, once a common companion, has become something close to an emergency to be resolved.

Yet boredom is more than an empty feeling. It is a signal, a kind of internal nudge that says the current activity no longer holds our attention and something else might. When we allow ourselves to sit with it, the mind begins to wander, and wandering is where many of our most useful thoughts take shape. Psychologists studying "default mode" activity have found that the brain's resting networks are busy with memory, planning, and imagining the future. Idle moments are not idle for the mind; they are when it sorts through what matters.

Consider how many good ideas arrive in the shower, on a long walk, or while staring out a train window. These are the moments when the mind is unoccupied enough to make new connections. Constant stimulation crowds out this quiet work. A mind that is never bored never has the chance to notice what it is actually thinking about, or to discover that it wants to think about something else entirely.

Boredom also teaches patience and tolerance for discomfort. To remain still with an unpleasant feeling, rather than fleeing it, builds a kind of emotional strength. Children who learn to occupy themselves in unstructured time often develop richer inner lives and greater self-reliance. Adults who never practice this skill may find that even mild discomfort becomes intolerable.

None of this means we should romanticize tedium or fill our days with drudgery. The point is not to suffer through boredom but to stop running from it reflexively. A few unscheduled minutes each day, left free of input, can return us to ourselves. In those minutes we may find that the world, for a moment, is quiet enough to hear our own thoughts again.

Walking a city at night changes the rules of being seen. By day, we move through streets as participants in a shared schedule, our faces half-hidden by the busyness around us. After dark, the city narrows. Shopfronts glow, streetlamps pool light on the pavement, and the people you pass become quieter, more particular, each one a small story walking in the opposite direction.

I have come to think of these walks as a kind of permission. Nobody expects much of you at eleven o'clock on a weeknight. You can slow down without explanation, stop to read a menu taped inside a restaurant window, or stand at a corner longer than necessary while the light changes twice. The obligations that fill the daytime thin out, and what remains is closer to attention.

There is also the matter of sound. Traffic does not vanish at night, but it softens and spaces itself out. A bus sighs at a stop. Somewhere above, a window opens and a snatch of music escapes before it closes again. Footsteps carry farther than they should, and you begin to hear your own rhythm, which is a strange and humbling thing to notice. In those moments the city feels less like a machine and more like a room with many people in it, all of them awake for reasons they keep to themselves.

Night walking also tends to loosen the mind. Without the constant pull of errands, the thoughts that surface are often the ones you had been postponing. A conversation you wish had gone differently replays itself under the sodium lights. A question about where you are heading, which seemed urgent at noon, becomes simply interesting. The rhythm of walking does something to memory, too, sorting the day's impressions into something more like a story.

Eventually the streets empty, and the last few figures ahead of you turn into side doors and disappear. You arrive home a little tired and a little clearer. The city has not solved anything, but it has offered a quiet space in which to think, and perhaps that is enough. Each night walk leaves something behind, a sharpened sense of the place and of yourself moving through it.

Why We Keep Old Letters

Somewhere in a drawer, or a shoebox on a closet shelf, there is usually a small stack of letters that nobody has the heart to throw away. The handwriting may have faded, the envelopes may have yellowed at the corners, and the paper may smell faintly of a house that no longer exists. Yet we keep them, often for decades, and it is worth asking why.

Part of the answer is that a letter is a trace of a particular moment. An email arrives, is read, and vanishes into a cluttered inbox. A handwritten letter required someone to sit down, choose words, and physically send something across distance. The pen pressed into the paper, the ink blotted where a hand paused, the crossed-out word that reveals a second thought. These details carry the writer's presence in a way that typed text rarely does. Keeping the letter is a way of keeping that presence close.

Letters also hold a version of ourselves we can no longer access. Rereading a letter we wrote at nineteen can be startling. The opinions seem earnest, the worries seem oddly specific, the plans now look naive or surprisingly wise. We discover that we have forgotten who we were, and the letter becomes a kind of witness. Keeping it means refusing to let that earlier self disappear entirely.

There is also the matter of the people who wrote to us. A letter from a grandparent, a friend who has died, or a former partner gives us their voice in a form that feels almost like conversation. We may not remember every fact of a relationship, but the phrasing, the jokes, and the sign-offs return us to how it felt to be loved or challenged by them. For many, these pages become a quiet archive of belonging.

Finally, we keep letters because they resist the flattening of memory. Our recollections reshape themselves over time, softening conflicts and inventing details. A letter does not change. It holds the exact words that were said, which can comfort us or correct us.

Perhaps that is the deepest reason. In a world of constant, disposable communication, an old letter reminds us that once, someone chose to reach across the distance for us, and we chose to keep their reaching.

Friendship is usually imagined as a thing between equals: people who grew up in the same years, share the same references, and move through life at the same pace. But some of the most surprising friendships I have seen cross the gap of decades, and they teach something the peer version cannot.

A friendship between generations begins with a kind of translation. A woman in her seventies and a man in his twenties may speak different dialects of the same language. He says "I'm going to cook for my roommates" and she hears a story about a kitchen she once shared with six strangers and a single temperamental stove. She says "We used to write letters," and he hears a fairy tale. Neither is wrong. The work of the friendship is the patient effort to hear what the other person means beneath the vocabulary.

What the older friend often offers is perspective earned through losses the younger one has not yet faced. She has buried parents, watched careers end, and learned which worries dissolve with time. This is not wisdom delivered as instruction. It shows up in small remarks, a shrug at a setback, a question asked at exactly the right moment. The younger friend, in return, offers the view from the middle of the river. He knows which technologies are changing daily, which ideas feel urgent, and what it is like to be unsure of the future rather than remembering the past. He keeps her curious. She keeps him from mistaking his anxieties for the end of the world.

These friendships also carry a particular tenderness because they are aware of their own limits. Everyone knows the age gap will eventually mean a goodbye that arrives too early for one of them. That knowledge can make the time feel heavier, but it can also make each conversation more deliberate. Without the assumption of decades ahead, people tend to say the true thing sooner.

Perhaps the deepest gift of such friendship is the reminder that a person is not a single age. The older friend is still the girl who climbed trees, and the younger friend is already the old man he will someday be, carrying the same hopes in a different body. Friendship across generations lets each person see themselves stretched across time, and that is a kind of companionship no contemporary can quite provide.

I used to read the way I drove on the highway, eyes always on the next exit. Finish the chapter, start the next one, keep the pages turning. Then one winter I got sick and couldn't do much but lie on the couch, and I picked up a old copy of *Middlemarch* that had been sitting on the shelf since college. I read four pages in an afternoon. I didn't mind. I was surprised that I didn't mind.

Slow reading is mostly a matter of noticing. You catch the sentence that turns on a single word, the one you'd have skated past at speed. You hear the rhythm of a paragraph and realize the writer has been building toward something for a full page. George Eliot takes her time describing a room, a face, a mild disappointment at breakfast, and by the time you reach the important scene you've come to care about these people more than you expected to.

Going slowly also means letting yourself stop. I put the book face down on my chest and stared at the ceiling for a while. A phrase kept circling back in my head. I wrote it on the back of an envelope, which is now bent and smudged and stuck in the book as a bookmark. That envelope has become one of my favorite things in the house, mostly because it records a moment when I wasn't hurrying.

There is a kind of pleasure in being slightly behind. Fast readers finish books and forget them. Slow readers carry sentences around for days, sometimes for years. You can't really compare the two experiences, any more than you can compare a meal eaten standing at the counter with one eaten across a table from someone you love.

I'm not sure I'll stay a slow reader. The habits of speed are stubborn, and my phone is always nearby with its small urgent demands. But I've started leaving a book out on the kitchen table, where I'll see it while the kettle heats. Sometimes I read one paragraph. Sometimes that's enough for the day.

The first thing I noticed was how quiet the airport felt. No one was waiting for me at the gate, no one needed my attention, and no one was there to share the sense of being somewhere new. For a moment that silence felt like a loss. By the end of the trip, it had become something I valued.

Travelling alone strips away the buffer of companionship. There is no one to pass the map to when you get lost, and no one to laugh with when a meal goes wrong. At first, every decision feels heavy because it belongs entirely to you: which train to catch, where to sleep, whether to turn down the narrow street or stay on the main road. That weight is real, but it is also clarifying. When you are the only one responsible for your choices, you start to notice what you actually want.

I spent most of my days wandering without a plan. I sat in a small square in a city whose language I could barely read and watched an old man feed pigeons with the seriousness of someone performing a ritual. I struck up conversations with strangers because there was nobody to talk to otherwise, and those brief exchanges turned out to be some of the most honest I have had. People open up to a solitary traveller in a way they rarely do with a group, perhaps because a lone person seems less like a tourist and more like someone worth hearing.

There were lonely evenings, too. Eating dinner at a table for one, I felt the familiar ache of wishing someone were across from me to share the moment. I have come to think that ache is useful. It reminds me how much I value connection, and it makes me more deliberate about the people I return to.

What travelling alone ultimately gave me was attention. Without distractions or obligations to someone else's schedule, I noticed light changing on old stone walls, the rhythm of a city waking up, and the small pleasure of finding a good coffee on my own terms. I learned that I can be my own company, and that solitude, when chosen, is less an absence than a kind of openness.

I came home tired, a little changed, and certain of one thing: the world is larger when you walk through it by yourself.

The bus pulls away from the curb, and for a moment everyone is thrown slightly forward, then settles. I have ridden the same route for years, and I have come to think of it less as a commute than as a standing invitation to look at strangers without being rude about it.

Public transport gives us a rare kind of permission. On a train, we are packed close together yet officially ignored. We may stare at a stranger's shoes, the paperback they are holding, or the way their thumb hovers over a phone screen without sending anything. Nobody asks what we are doing. We are simply two or forty people sharing a space for twelve minutes.

What I notice most is how people hold themselves when they think no one is looking, which is a strange thing to say about a room full of people. A woman in a yellow raincoat sits with her bag clutched on her lap, eyes closed, lips moving slightly as though rehearsing a conversation. An older man reads the same page of a newspaper for three stops. Two teenagers share one pair of earphones, each leaning toward the other to catch the song. Their small arrangement feels like the most private thing in the car.

These glimpses unsettle me a little, because they remind me how much of a life is invisible. I know nothing about these people beyond a few seconds of posture and expression, yet I build stories out of them anyway. The woman in the raincoat has had a bad morning. The old man is lonely, or perhaps just content with a quiet routine. The teenagers are in love, or about to be. My stories are almost certainly wrong, and that is part of the pleasure. They are a reminder that everyone on that train is the protagonist of a story I will never read.

There is also something humbling in it. We are all, for a short while, dependent on the same machine, the same schedule, and the same fragile agreement to stay in our seats until the doors open. Watching others reminds me that I am one ordinary passenger among many, carrying my own unseen worries.

When my stop arrives, I stand, nudge past a sleeping man's knees, and step onto the platform. The train hums away, carrying its unknown passengers toward their own destinations. I rarely learn how their days turn out. Still, for those few minutes together, we shared a small and ordinary world, and I am grateful for having seen it.

On Idleness

There is a particular kind of afternoon that has become rare: the kind where nothing is required of me. The light moves across the floor, a cup of tea cools beside me, and I do not reach for my phone or compose a list in my head. For most of my adult life I have treated such hours as wasted, as gaps waiting to be filled. Lately I have started to suspect that they were the opposite.

We tend to speak of idleness as an absence, the empty space where productivity should be. But the word itself is revealing. It comes from the Old English *idel*, meaning empty or vain, and that is how our culture has taught us to regard it. Yet an empty vessel is not necessarily a useless one. A pond that is never stirred becomes clear enough to show the sky.

Idleness gives the mind room to wander, and wandering is where many of our most useful thoughts are born. A problem left unattended for a day often unknots itself while we are doing nothing at all. A half-remembered face returns. A sentence we have been struggling to write arrives whole while we stare out a window. Psychologists studying "default mode" activity have found that the brain's background networks, active when we are not focused on a task, are involved in memory, planning, and imagining the future. Idleness, it turns out, is not the switching off of thought but a different mode of it.

There is also a moral dimension we rarely discuss. To be idle is to be unclaimed by obligation for a while, to be simply present in the world rather than useful to it. Many traditions have honored this. The Sabbath asks people to stop working. Monastic rules set aside hours for contemplation. Even the old notion of *otium*, which the Romans contrasted with *negotium*, the busy labor that defined public life, suggested that leisure was the space where a person became fully human, able to study, reflect, and converse freely.

I do not want to romanticize it. Idleness can slide into avoidance, and boredom can curdle into despair. The difference, I think, lies in attention. Idle time becomes generative when we sit with it openly, without numbing distraction, willing to see what surfaces. Ten minutes of scrolling is not idleness; it is a small anxious escape from ourselves.

So I am trying to practice a smaller, humbler discipline: to leave a few empty spaces in the day on purpose, and to let them remain empty. The tea goes cold. The light shifts. Something quiet occurs to me, and I let it stay.

Autumn reminds me that everything is always leaving and returning at once. The maples on my street have turned the color of embers, and their leaves drift down in slow spirals, landing on sidewalks and car windshields with no hurry at all. I used to think of autumn as a sad season, a countdown to winter. Now I see it as a kind of honest letting go, a reminder that nothing is meant to hold on forever.

Winter asks a different question: what remains when the noise falls away? The bare branches reveal the architecture of every tree, shapes hidden all summer under their abundance. Frost writes patterns on the window that no one designed, and the quiet of snowfall makes even a busy city feel briefly like a held breath. I have learned that winter is not empty. It is where roots work in the dark, where stillness does its slow repair.

Spring arrives like a argument the earth has been rehearsing for months. The first crocuses push through thawing soil, and the air carries a smell of wet ground and new growth. Every year I am surprised by how quickly the world turns green again, as though it has been waiting for permission. Spring teaches patience with the unfinished, since blossoms are fragile and frost can still return.

Summer is the season of fullness, when light lingers past dinner and the days seem to stretch like taffy. It tempts us to believe the warmth will never end. Yet even in summer, the garden is quietly preparing its seeds, and the cicadas begin their long chorus toward the coming change.

Looking across the four seasons, I notice that none of them is the real one. Each is a passage, a doorway into the next. Perhaps that is the lesson they offer: to live fully in whatever season we are in, while trusting that the wheel keeps turning. The leaves fall so that the branches may rest, and the rest makes room for the bloom. Seasons remind us that change is not a loss but the shape of life itself.

Dear Me at Sixteen,

You're going to feel like the world is ending over things that will barely matter in five years. The argument with your best friend, the grade you didn't get, the way your voice sounds on recordings. Let yourself feel it, but know that most of it will fade faster than you expect.

Some things I need you to hear now. Start saving money, even small amounts. Future you will be grateful in ways that are hard to explain. Learn to cook one meal well. Read the books that feel boring at first, because they'll stay with you longer than the ones everyone talks about.

Be kinder to your body. You'll spend years being hard on it, and it has carried you through more than you realize. Get outside more. Walk without a destination.

About the people: some friendships will end, and that's okay. Not every goodbye is a failure. Tell the people you love that you love them, even when it feels awkward. Call your grandmother more. You'll wish you had.

You don't have to know what you want to do with your life yet. Nobody does, including most of the adults who seem to. Try things. Be curious. Say yes to a few things that scare you.

And when you fail, and you will, notice that you survived it. That's something you'll keep relearning, so you might as well start now.

You are more capable than you believe, and less alone than you feel.

With love and a little more perspective,
Me at Thirty-Something

Dear Maya,

I've been thinking about you constantly since we last spoke, and I wanted to put some of it on paper, because some things are easier to say when you don't have to find the right words on the spot.

I'm so sorry about your mother. I know no sentence can carry the weight of losing her, and I won't pretend I understand exactly what this feels like from the inside. But I remember how she laughed at her own jokes before she got to the punchline, and how she always asked whether we'd eaten, even when we'd just come from dinner. Those small things are hers, and they're still here.

Grief doesn't follow a schedule. Some days you may feel steady, and then a song or a smell or a stray phone number will knock the air out of you. That isn't a sign you're doing it wrong. It's what love looks like when it has nowhere to go.

You don't have to be strong for me, or for anyone, right now. You don't have to answer my messages quickly or make plans you don't want to make. If you want company, I'll come sit with you and say nothing at all. If you want to talk about her, I'd love to hear anything you're ready to share, even the ordinary stories.

Please take care of yourself, too. Eat something, drink some water, and let yourself rest even when sleep won't come.

I'm here, whenever you need me, for as long as you need me.

With love,
Elena

Dear Sam,

I keep starting this letter and deleting it, because every version sounds like a greeting card, and you deserve better than that. So I'll just say it plainly: I'm so sorry about your dad.

I know there's nothing I can write that makes this smaller. I'm not going to try. I just wanted you to know I'm thinking about you, and that I think about him too. He was the one who taught us both how to back a trailer up without yelling, and who wouldn't let either of us leave a barbecue without a plate of something. I still can't believe he's gone.

You don't have to be okay right now. You don't have to answer this, or call, or be the strong one for anybody. If you want to talk about him, I'd love that. If you want to sit in silence on the phone for ten minutes, I'm good with that too. If you want me to just show up with food and leave it on the porch, say the word.

Some days it's going to hit you out of nowhere, like at the grocery store or when you hear a song he liked. That's normal. It doesn't mean you're falling apart. It means you loved him.

Eat something today, even if it's just toast. Sleep when you can. And let people help, even the clumsy ones.

I love you, man. I'm here.

Dana

Dear Ms. Carter,

I wanted to take a moment to thank you for everything you have done for me this year. Looking back, I can see how much your guidance has shaped the way I think, learn, and approach challenges.

From the first day of class, you made every student feel welcome and capable. You never rushed past a question, no matter how simple it seemed. When I struggled with the research project in the fall, you did not simply hand me the answers. Instead, you asked questions that helped me find my own way, and that patience taught me more than any single assignment could have.

I am also grateful for the way you challenged me to be honest in my writing. Your comments on my essays were often tough, but they always pushed me to think more carefully and to say exactly what I meant. I have carried that lesson into every class since, and I know my work is stronger because of it.

Beyond the material itself, you showed me what it looks like to care about the people you teach. Your encouragement on the days I felt discouraged meant more than you may realize. You reminded me that effort matters as much as results, and that mistakes are part of learning.

Thank you for your time, your kindness, and your belief in me. I hope you know how much your work matters, and that the lessons you taught will stay with me for a long time.

With sincere gratitude,

Alex Norlind

Dear Aunt Margaret,

I hope this letter finds you well and warm as the cold weather settles in here. I wanted to share some news about the harvest, which finished last week.

The corn came in better than we dared to hope. After the dry spell in July, I worried we would lose much of the east field, but the late August rains saved the ears, and most of them filled out well. The soybeans were steadier, though the yield per acre was a little lower than last year. Dad would have been pleased with the wheat, which we planted in the fall and which gave us a clean, heavy grain at the elevator.

The hardest part was the weather in October. We had three days of rain in a row just as we reached the back forty, and the combine sat idle while the ground turned to mud. Still, Tom and the Miller boys pitched in, and we got it all in before the first hard frost.

Things were not all work, though. On the last evening, we set up a long table in the barn and had a supper for everyone who helped. Mrs. Hale brought her apple pie, and the children ran between the hay bales until it got too dark to see. It reminded me of the harvests when you and Mom used to visit, and I missed you both.

Next year I plan to try a new rotation on the north fields, and I would love your advice on it. Please write when you can, and tell me how things are going in the city.

With love,

Ruth

Dear Uncle Walt,

We finished bringing in the beans last Thursday, and I'm pleased to say the yield came in better than I expected. The north forty gave us about forty bushels to the acre, which is more than Dad ever got off that ground, though he'd probably tell you the rain in August had a lot to do with it. It sure did.

The corn was a different story. The early rains washed out the low spots near the creek, so we lost a good strip of it, and the stalks along the fence line never really filled out. Still, the rest of the field made decent ears. Ray from the co-op came out to look at it and said the moisture numbers were fine, so we should get a fair price at the elevator if the market holds through December.

The wheat went in on time this fall, which helps. Ma's knee has been bothering her, so I've been doing most of the driving on the combine, and I think I finally got the hang of the auger without knocking the header off on the gravel road. Jenny helped with the grain cart on the weekends, and the kids liked riding along on the tractor until about four in the afternoon, when they started complaining about the dust.

We've got the cattle moved down to the winter pasture now, and the hay barn is about two-thirds full. If the weather cooperates, we should be able to get through the cold months without buying any more feed.

Tell Aunt Carol we said hello, and that the pie she sent for Thanksgiving last year is still talked about in this house. Maybe you two can make the drive out after the new year. The coffee's always on.

Your nephew,
Dale

The wind had been pushing rain sideways since dusk, and Tomas Vell was halfway through trimming the lamp wick when the beam swept across something that did not belong to the rocks. He stopped, wick in hand, and waited for the next pass of light. There it was again: a dark shape, low and still, at the edge of the tide line where the granite broke into black teeth.

He climbed down the iron stairs without bothering with his coat. The stairs were slick, and his knees complained at every turn, but he had kept this light for twenty-two years and knew every step by its ring under his boots.

The figure was a woman, or at least it looked like one from the wet outline of her shoulders. She lay on her side with one arm folded under her head, as though she had simply lain down to rest and the sea had decided to keep her company. Her hair was plastered across her face. A canvas bag, torn at one strap, lay a few feet off, half-buried in kelp.

Tomas knelt beside her and pressed two fingers to her neck. For a long moment there was nothing but rain and the grumble of water in the channel. Then a faint pulse stirred against his fingertips, quick and stubborn.

"Hey," he said, and his voice came out rougher than he intended. "Can you hear me?"

Her eyelids fluttered. Her lips moved, but the only sound was a breath that might have been a word.

Tomas glanced up at the lighthouse, its beam wheeling steadily over the water as if nothing had happened. The radio in the keeper's room would reach the mainland in an hour, if the storm allowed it. The boat would take longer.

He shrugged out of his soaked sweater, wrapped it around her shoulders, and gathered her up with a grunt. She weighed less than he expected.

"Don't you dare die on my rocks," he muttered, and began the long climb back toward the light.

Mira learned to hear the plants the summer her grandmother's hands stopped being steady enough for the garden. It did not come as a revelation. It came as a headache, a low static behind her eyes, and then, one afternoon in the back of the greenhouse, a thin, sour murmur from the tomato vines that sounded almost like someone clearing their throat.

*Thirsty,* the tomatoes said. Not in words, exactly. More like a shape pressing against the inside of her skull.

She dropped the watering can. Water pooled on the concrete floor and ran toward the drain, and the vines went quiet, as if embarrassed.

"Mira?" her grandmother called from the doorway. "You're letting it all out."

"The tomatoes are thirsty," Mira said, and then felt foolish, because her grandmother only smiled the way she smiled at weather reports.

But the tomatoes were thirsty. Mira knelt, pressed her palm to the soil, and the murmur sharpened into something almost grateful. Beneath it ran other sounds: the slow, patient hum of the basil, which thought in long, sweet loops about sunlight; the bitter, clipped complaints of the dandelions along the fence, who did not like being pulled and never forgot it.

She had expected silence. Instead the garden was crowded.

Over the following weeks she learned their vocabularies, which were nothing like human ones. The roses thought in scent. The ivy on the north wall thought in patience so vast it made her dizzy. The old oak by the road thought almost nothing at all, only a deep, rooted contentment that felt like standing in a warm lake.

She told no one at school. She told no one at all, except the basil, which seemed to enjoy being told things.

Then, in late August, she heard the lilac by the gate begin to mourn.

Dust had settled on the bench outside the Harlow Street precinct for so long that Walt Brennan no longer noticed it. He sat there anyway most mornings, coffee going cold in a paper cup, watching the city wake up without him. Thirty-one years on the job had taught him that people reveal themselves in small gestures, and he had catalogued his own for three years now: the way he still checked his jacket pocket for a notebook he no longer carried, the way his hand drifted toward a phone that rang less each month.

The envelope arrived on a Tuesday. No stamp, just his name in careful block letters and a return address that belonged to a laundromat two miles east, one he had walked past a hundred times on the way to cases that were long closed.

Inside was a photograph, black and white, the kind developed in a darkroom instead of printed at a kiosk. It showed a loading dock behind the old Meridian Cold Storage building, the one that had been demolished the spring after he retired. In the corner of the frame, half-hidden by a stack of crates, a woman's shoe lay on its side.

He knew that shoe. He had written it into a report eighteen years ago, in a case the department had been happy to close without a second look. Walt turned the photo over. On the back, in the same careful hand, were four words.

*You never finished it.*

He set the photograph on the bench beside him and looked up at the gray November sky. His knee ached, the way it did before rain. For the first time in three years, the familiar restlessness in his chest felt less like grief and more like a question waiting for an answer.

Walt folded the envelope, slid it into his jacket, and stood up slowly. He did not finish the coffee. He did not need to. He had a feeling the day was going to be a long one, and for the first time in a long while, he was glad of it.

The florist was the first to say it out loud, which Marnie thought was rude, considering she had already been paid.

"He's not here yet," the florist said, holding a bundle of white ranunculus like a baby she'd been asked to mind for a minute. "Is that normal?"

It was twelve-forty. The ceremony was at one. Marnie's mother had cried twice in the vestibule, once happily and once the way she cried when a casserole dish cracked, and Aunt Phyllis was out in the parking lot on the phone with someone who was definitely not the groom.

Marnie stood in the back room of the Grange Hall with her veil pinned crooked and a plastic cup of ginger ale going flat in her hand. Someone had hung a banner over the sink that said FOREVER STARTS TODAY. The letters were cut from felt, and one of the Y's was sagging. She kept looking at it.

Ben was supposed to be here at noon for photos. At 11:58, his brother Dale had texted her a thumbs-up emoji. At the time she'd taken it as a joke about nerves, because Ben was the kind of man who checked the weather three times a day and then wore a sweater anyway. Dale had been with Ben at the bar until almost midnight. Marnie remembered thinking that was a nice thing for brothers to do.

Her phone buzzed. Not Ben. Her sister.

*Are you okay? Want me to come back there*

Marnie watched the three dots appear, vanish, and appear again.

She didn't answer. She set the ginger ale on the counter beside a tray of unlit tealights and listened through the wall to the piano, playing the same four bars of the processional over and over, played by a woman who had not been told yet.

The library smelled of radiator dust and old paper, the way it always did on Thursdays, and Owen had claimed the same corner table since September. He liked the quiet. He liked that nobody asked what he was reading.

The book was a battered field guide to birds, its spine cracked white in a dozen places. He pulled it from the shelf only because the cover was blue, and blue was the color of the sky his grandmother used to point at when she named the swallows.

Tucked between pages 112 and 113 was an envelope. It was cream-colored, soft at the corners, and sealed with a stamp that had been licked and pressed so long ago the glue had gone brown. On the front, in careful slanted handwriting, someone had written a single name: *Margaret*.

Owen looked around. Mrs. Ellery was stamping returns at the front desk. Two girls were whispering over a laptop near the windows. No one was watching him.

He turned the envelope over. The flap was unsealed. It had never been sealed at all, he realized, or someone had opened it and tucked it back in, the way you'd keep a secret you couldn't bring yourself to burn.

Inside was a single sheet of paper folded into thirds. The first line read:

*If you are reading this, then the swallows came back, and I was right to wait.*

Owen read it again. Then he read the date at the bottom, a date from before his mother was born, and felt the hair on his arms lift, as though the room had grown a little colder.

He glanced at the book's checkout card in the back pocket. The last name stamped there was his own grandmother's.

The train had been moving for three days, and Vera had stopped counting the stations. They ran together now, each one a platform of packed snow, a yellow lamp, a babushka selling smoked fish from a bucket, and then the long exhale of the brakes and the slow pull eastward again. Somewhere past Krasnoyarsk she had begun to think of the carriage as a country of its own, with its own weather, its own hours, its own laws about who got the lower bunk.

Her compartment held four. A geologist from Tomsk who snored in short, polite bursts. A young soldier who kept his boots on and his eyes shut. And across from her, by the window, an old man in a grey wool coat who had boarded at Perm and had not, as far as Vera could tell, spoken a single word since.

She had decided he was a retired surveyor. Something about the way he studied the landscape, lips moving very slightly, as though he were measuring it against a map only he could see. Each morning he unwrapped a boiled egg with great care, peeled it in one long spiral, and ate it while watching the birches go by.

The light was going now, thin and copper over the taiga. The snow on the far hills had turned the color of weak tea. Vera pressed her forehead to the glass and felt the cold come through it like a verdict.

She had a letter in her coat pocket, folded four times, its corners soft from handling. She had read it so often that she no longer needed to unfold it. The address on the envelope was a village she could not yet picture, a name she had only ever seen written in her mother's hand.

"Nearly there," said the old man suddenly, not looking at her. His voice was dry as paper. "Another eleven hours, if the locomotive behaves."

Vera turned from the window. "Do you know the village?"

He was quiet for a long moment, and the train swayed through a curve, and somewhere ahead a whistle sounded, long and low and lonely across the white.

"I knew someone who did," he said.

The first thing Marisol noticed was that the lemon tasted like nothing at all. She had squeezed it over the sole the way she had ten thousand times before, and the brightness simply didn't arrive. It was like biting into a cold, wet paper towel that happened to be yellow.

She set the knife down and waited. Maybe it was the fish. Maybe it was the flu she'd shaken off last week, the one that had left her sleeping in her coat on the back stairs. Her sous chef, Teodor, was watching her from the pass with the careful face people use around a dog that has started limping.

"Taste this," she said, and handed him the spoon.

He did, and his eyebrows rose in a way that told her he was being generous. "It's good, Chef."

"It's *salt*, Teo. It's salt and fat and a little heat. Where's the sorrel?"

"It's in there."

"I know it's in there. I can't find it."

The dining room was filling. She could hear the scrape of chairs, the clink of someone's wine glass against a bread plate, a woman laughing too loudly at a joke that had clearly been told before. Eighty covers tonight. Her name was on the awning in gold letters that had cost more than her first car. Every bit of it rested on the tongue she was no longer sure she had.

She picked up a leaf of basil from the cutting board and pressed it between her teeth. Green, bruised, faintly bitter, the way it had always been. Except there was no flavor of anything. It was texture only, a limp rasp against her molars, like chewing a page from a phone book.

Teodor cleared his throat. "Should I call Dr. Adeyemi?"

Marisol looked at the ticket rail, where forty-one orders waited in neat white slips, each one a small demand that someone, somewhere, would be satisfied. She thought of her grandmother, who had cooked by smell alone after the cataracts took her sight, and who had once told her that the nose was a liar but the mouth never was.

"Not yet," Marisol said. "Fire the sole."

The bus pulled into the gravel loop at 9:40 and nobody got off right away. That was the first thing Dana noticed. Every other morning for the last three weeks, the kids had been spilling out of the doors before the brakes finished hissing, screaming somebody's name, already halfway to the lake. Today they just sat there, looking out the windows at the cabins like they were trying to memorize them.

"Come on, bugs," Dana said, standing up in the aisle and grabbing the rail. "Last day. Nobody gets to be slow on the last day."

Nobody laughed. Tyler Ruiz, who had cried on Tuesday because a moth landed on his sleeve, was holding his duffel in both arms like a pillow. Priya had her friendship bracelet on her wrist, the one she'd been making for Marisol since week one. She'd finished it at 2 a.m. under a flashlight, and Dana had pretended not to notice.

Outside, the flagpole rope clanked against the metal. Somebody had already taken the flag down, which meant the ceremony was over, which meant the morning was just the long slow part where everyone pretended they weren't leaving.

"Okay," Dana said. "Who wants to be first off?"

Silence. Then a small voice from the back: "Can we go around the lake one more time?"

It was Marisol. Of course it was.

Dana looked at the clock above the driver's seat, which had been running four minutes fast since June. Four minutes. That was all they had before the parents started showing up in their clean cars with their coffee and their questions.

"Yeah," she said, and her voice came out rougher than she wanted. "Yeah, okay. One more time."

The morning the letter arrived, Mayor Dale Hendricks was already halfway through his second cup of coffee, watching the frost retreat from the windows of Harlow Falls Town Hall. He recognized the envelope before he read the name on it. The paper was the same heavy cream stock his brother had always favored, and the postmark was from Cedar Ridge, three hundred miles north, where nobody in Harlow Falls had any reason to look.

He set the coffee down carefully, the way you'd set down something that might go off.

Outside, the town was waking up. Mrs. Pruitt was sweeping the steps of the bakery. Two teenagers on bicycles wobbled past the courthouse, shouting about a football game. The flag over the post office snapped in a wind that smelled of woodsmoke and wet leaves. Everything looked exactly as it had for twenty-two years, which was the whole point.

Dale slid a letter opener under the flap. Inside was a single sheet, folded once, with four words written in blue ink: *We need to talk.*

He didn't need to read the rest. He knew who had written it, and he knew what it meant. Somewhere in the back of his mind, a door he had bricked shut two decades ago was beginning, very quietly, to crack.

He folded the letter, slipped it into his jacket pocket, and straightened his tie in the reflection of the dark glass. Then he picked up the ribbon-cutting schedule from his desk, smiled at nobody, and walked out to greet the people who trusted him.

The ferry horn sounded twice across the harbor, long and low, and Walter Vance felt it in his teeth before he heard it fully. He was still two hundred yards up the hill, his suitcase bumping against his shin with every stride, the cardboard box of his late wife's cookbooks wedged under one arm.

"Wait," he said to no one. His voice came out thin.

The gangway was already rising. He could see Deckhand Ruiz, a boy he'd once tipped a dollar for carrying groceries, lift his hand in a half-apology before turning away. The ramp folded upward like a closing mouth, and the white hull began its slow reverse from the pier.

Walter stopped at the top of the lot and bent over, hands on his knees. His breath tore in and out. Below him, the water went from gray to silver as the ferry pulled free, its wake spreading in neat, widening lines toward the breakwater.

He had timed it. He was certain he had timed it. He had checked his watch at the diner, then again at the bus shelter, then once more at the crosswalk, and each time the numbers had seemed to promise him ten minutes more than he had.

Behind him, a car door slammed. Somebody laughed at something on a phone. The gulls kept up their argument over a crust of bread on the asphalt, unbothered.

Walter straightened slowly and looked at the box under his arm. The top flap had come loose, and a corner of his wife's handwriting peeked out from a recipe card, the ink blurred from years of kitchen steam. *Dorothy's Lemon Bars. Don't overbake, Walt.*

He almost laughed. Instead he sat down on the curb, set the box beside him, and watched the ferry grow smaller on the water, its lights blinking out one by one as the fog rolled in from the north.

The rain had been falling for three days when the river finally gave up its banks. Maren Tollef stood at the kitchen window and watched the water creep across the lower field, silver and patient, swallowing the fence posts one by one. Behind her the kettle ticked as it cooled. Nobody had bothered to fill it again.

Below the ridge, Haldsby lay in a fold of land that had always been more water than ground. Forty-one houses, a chapel with a crooked spire, a schoolhouse with one teacher and eleven children, and the single road that linked them to the rest of the country. That road was under two feet of brown current now. The bridge at Kessel had gone sometime before dawn. Nobody had seen it go. They had only heard the sound, a long groan like a ship's hull, and then a silence that felt wrong.

Maren's brother Anders came in stamping mud from his boots, his face gray with cold and something harder to name. "Radio's dead," he said. "Phone's dead. Harald rode up to the pass on his horse at six, said he'd send word. He hasn't come back."

She nodded and kept looking at the water. There was a strange calm in her, the kind that arrives after fear has been used up. "How long can we hold out?"

"Depends on the stores. Depends on whether it rises." He pulled off his gloves. "Depends on whether anyone's looking for us."

Outside, the wind shifted and drove the rain sideways against the glass. Somewhere down in the village a dog barked, once, twice, then fell quiet. Maren thought of the children in the schoolhouse, of old Greta who could not climb stairs, of the chapel bell that no one had rung since the flood warnings began.

"They'll look," she said. She wanted to believe it. "They always look eventually."

Anders didn't answer. He crossed to the cupboard, took down the lamp, and began to trim its wick with steady hands, the way their father used to before every storm. The small flame caught and grew, and for a moment the room held only its warm circle of light, while beyond the glass the dark water kept rising.

Marjorie had been dead for eleven days before she managed to knock anything off a shelf, and when she finally did it, the mug hit the linoleum and didn't even break. It just rolled under the fridge. She hovered over the spot for a while, feeling the way you feel after you've sneezed in a meeting. Nobody screamed. Nobody even looked up from the crossword.

The new tenants were a couple in their thirties, the kind who had a sourdough starter named after a Tolkien character. The husband, Dev, was the one who noticed things. He'd stand in the kitchen with his coffee and say, "Huh," to nobody, and Marjorie would think, *that's the spirit*, and then forget what she was supposed to do next.

She had read the books, or at least the one she'd found at the library sale before the cancer took her ability to drive. It said you could move a teacup across a table with focused intent. It said the cold spots were the easy part. It did not say anything about how tiring it was to concentrate on a teacup for four minutes straight while your own thoughts kept drifting off to whether you'd turned off the stove in 1997.

Her daughter, Pam, had asked her once, back when Marjorie was still alive and lucid, what she wanted to do after. "Haunt the Safeway," Marjorie had said. "Mess with the self-checkout." Pam had laughed. Marjorie had meant it, sort of.

Now she was here, in her own old kitchen, which somebody had painted a color she'd have called "hospital mint." The cabinets were the same. The window over the sink still stuck. She'd tried to open it the first night and got nothing but a faint rattle, which Dev had blamed on the wind.

She sat down on the floor, back against the dishwasher, and thought: eleven days, one mug, and a man who says "huh." Not exactly the stuff of legend.

"Is the salmon fresh?"

"It's fresh. It came in today."

"Today or today-today?"

"Today, sir. Tuesday's fish is Wednesday's fish's older brother."

"That's not reassuring."

"No, sir. It isn't."

"Yes, sir." He turned to go, then stopped. "For what it's worth, she'll probably come in a few minutes. They always do."

"How do you know?"

"Because I've been standing here since five, and I've seen everybody come in eventually."
