**City Council Approves Expansion of Bike Lane Network**

The city council voted 6-1 Tuesday night to extend the downtown bike lane network by 4.2 miles, a project supporters say will make cycling safer and more practical for residents across the city.

The new lanes will connect the existing Riverside Trail to the Eastgate business district and the Northside library, with protected barriers installed along the busiest stretches of Main Street and Oak Avenue. Construction is expected to begin in the spring and finish within 18 months.

"People have been asking for this for years," said Councilmember Janet Ortiz, who sponsored the measure. "Parents want their kids to ride to school safely, and commuters want an alternative to sitting in traffic. This gives them that choice."

The project is funded through a combination of state transportation grants and municipal bond money, totaling roughly $6.8 million. Council members who opposed the measure raised concerns about the cost and the loss of about 60 street parking spaces along Oak Avenue.

Councilmember Tom Haverly cast the lone dissenting vote. "I support cycling, but we need to make sure local businesses aren't hurt by losing parking," he said after the meeting. He requested that the city conduct a six-month review of foot traffic and sales in affected areas.

Business owners along Oak Avenue were divided. Maria Chen, who runs a bakery near the proposed route, said she worries about deliveries but welcomes the increased foot traffic. "If people can bike here, they'll stop in more often," she said.

Public comment was heavily in favor of the plan, with more than 40 residents speaking during the three-hour session. Several noted that the city's bike lane network has remained largely unchanged for a decade.

Construction planning will begin in January, and the city will hold community meetings in December to gather input on specific lane placements.

**Lincoln Robotics Team Takes Top Honors at Regional Championship**

*Staff Report*

A team of high school students from Riverbend High School brought home the first-place trophy from this weekend's Northern Valley Regional Robotics Competition, outperforming 34 teams from across the region.

The Riverbend squad, known as the Iron Otters, earned the title after their robot completed the most successful combination of tasks in the event's final round. The machine, designed and built over a six-week season, collected and stacked foam blocks, navigated an obstacle course, and launched a ball into a high goal with consistent accuracy.

"We spent a lot of late nights in the shop, and there were plenty of moments when things didn't work the first time," said team captain Maya Ellison, a senior. "What made the difference was that everyone kept testing and fixing until it worked."

The team's engineering mentor, science teacher David Kwan, praised the students for their teamwork and problem-solving. "These kids made every decision together, from the drivetrain design to the programming," Kwan said. "I'm most proud of how they supported each other when they hit setbacks."

The Iron Otters will now advance to the state championship in March. Team members said they plan to use the coming months to refine the robot's battery system and improve its speed on the course.

The regional event drew spectators from several nearby towns, and organizers said this year's competition was the largest in its history. Local business sponsors who helped fund the team's parts and travel were recognized during the awards ceremony.

The Iron Otters will hold a fundraising pancake breakfast at the Riverbend Community Center on December 6. Proceeds will support the team's trip to the state event.

**New North Wing Opens at Riverside Community Hospital**

RIVERSIDE — Riverside Community Hospital welcomed patients, staff, and local leaders Monday to the grand opening of its new four-story North Wing, a $48 million expansion that adds 60 inpatient beds and modernized emergency care facilities to the county's largest medical center.

The wing features a 20-bed emergency department, separate entrances for ambulance and walk-in patients, and a dedicated pediatric unit with family sleeping quarters. Hospital officials said the design was shaped by feedback from nurses and patients, with single-occupancy rooms and wider corridors to accommodate hospital beds and visiting families.

"This building was designed around the people who use it every day," said Dr. Helen Marsh, the hospital's chief executive. "Our patients deserve space to heal, and our staff deserve the tools to care for them well."

The expansion was funded through a combination of a 2022 voter-approved bond measure, private donations, and state health infrastructure grants. Construction began in early 2024 and was completed ahead of schedule and within budget, according to project manager Luis Ortega.

County Commissioner Dana Whitfield joined a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the main entrance, calling the project "a milestone for everyone who lives in this region." Residents who need medical care no longer have to travel to neighboring cities for many specialized services, she noted.

The North Wing is expected to create about 150 new jobs, including nursing, technical, and support positions. Hospital officials said recruitment is ongoing and that applications are available through the hospital's website.

Tours of the new wing will be offered to the public every Saturday through December. The hospital's emergency department will begin operating from the new space on Thursday.

**Local Library Launches Seed Lending Program to Boost Community Gardens**

*Hollow Creek Public Library Introduces "Seed Library" Initiative*

Hollow Creek Public Library has launched a seed lending program, giving residents free access to a collection of vegetable, herb, and flower seeds. The initiative, which opened its doors this week, is designed to help local gardeners save money and encourage sustainable growing practices across the community.

Under the new system, patrons can browse the seed catalog at the library's reference desk and "check out" up to five packets per visit. Unlike traditional library books, seeds are not returned in their original form. Borrowers are encouraged to grow plants, collect seeds from their harvest, and return a portion to the library at the end of the season.

"The idea is simple: share what you grow, and the library keeps the collection going," said Maria Delgado, the library's community outreach coordinator. "We want to build a cycle where neighbors help one another grow food and beauty."

The seeds were donated by local farmers, master gardeners, and members of the Hollow Creek Garden Club. Heirloom varieties, including tomatoes, beans, and squash, make up a significant portion of the collection.

Library staff will also offer free workshops on seed saving, soil preparation, and composting. The first session takes place Saturday at 10 a.m. in the community room.

"Gardening can be expensive, and not everyone has room for a plot," Delgado said. "This program lets anyone with a windowsill or a small yard take part."

The seed library is open during regular library hours. Residents interested in donating seeds can drop them off at the front desk, with envelopes labeled by variety and growing information.

**Hundreds Lace Up for Little Hearts at Riverside Charity Marathon**

RIVERSIDE — Under gray skies and a light drizzle, more than 600 runners gathered at Millbrook Park on Sunday morning for the third annual Little Hearts Marathon, raising funds for the Riverside Children's Fund, which supports pediatric care and family services across the county.

Participants ran a full 26.2-mile course, a half marathon, or a 5K fun run that wound through the Riverside Greenway and along the river. Many wore bright bibs decorated by local schoolchildren, and several teams carried handmade signs bearing the names of young patients they were running for.

"Every mile means something to us," said Dana Whitfield, who completed the full marathon for the second year in a row. "Last year, my nephew spent six weeks at Riverside Children's Hospital. Seeing the staff on the course today reminded me why we do this."

Volunteers handed out water and oranges at every mile marker, while the Riverside High School marching band played along the final stretch near the park's main gate.

Organizers announced that the event raised more than $184,000, surpassing last year's total by nearly 20 percent. Funds will go toward a new family lounge in the hospital's pediatric wing and expanded transportation assistance for families traveling long distances for treatment.

"This community shows up every year," said Fund director Marcus Ellery as he crossed the finish line to cheers. "Today, they showed up for kids who need it most."

Registration for next year's race opens in January. Details are available at the Riverside Children's Fund website.

**Runners raise $41,000 for children's hospital fund at Cedar Falls Marathon**

CEDAR FALLS — About 620 runners finished the Cedar Falls Marathon on Saturday, and organizers say the race brought in $41,200 for the Riverside Children's Fund, the largest total in the event's nine-year history.

The course started at the courthouse square at 7 a.m. under gray skies and a light drizzle that cleared by mid-morning. Runners looped through the Millbrook trail and finished on Main Street, where a crowd of several hundred cheered them across the line.

"I didn't think about the cold until about mile 20, and then I thought about it a lot," said Dana Whitfield, a nurse at Cedar Falls General who ran her third marathon. She said she ran for a patient she met last spring. "Kids in that ward have it way harder than I do on a bad day."

Race director Tom Okafor said most of the money came from pledges collected over the summer, with the rest from registration fees and a bake sale run by the Lincoln Middle School band. "We had more sponsors than ever, and a lot of people who just showed up to hand out water," Okafor said.

The Riverside Children's Fund pays for travel costs for families whose kids are treated at hospitals in the regional center, about an hour away. Director Lila Brandt said the money would help cover gas, hotel stays, and meals for about 150 families next year.

Winner of the men's race was Eli Sorensen, 27, of Hollis, who finished in 2:38:14. Mara Kellerman was first among women in 3:01:52.

Registration for next year opens January 5.

**Rare Western Tanager Draws Birders to Maplewood Park**

Bird enthusiasts converged on Maplewood Park this weekend after a vibrant visitor appeared in the oak grove near the duck pond: a male western tanager, a species rarely seen this far east in November.

Local birder Dana Whitfield spotted the bird Saturday morning while walking her dog. "At first I thought it was a tropical songbird that had escaped from someone's aviary," she said. "The red head and bright yellow body stood out against the gray branches. I grabbed my binoculars and knew right away it was something special."

Western tanagers typically migrate through the western United States and Canada in spring and summer, wintering in Mexico and Central America. Experts say a late-season stray like this one is uncommon but not unheard of, often blown off course by storms or following unusual weather patterns.

By Sunday afternoon, about 40 birders had gathered along the park's trails with cameras and spotting scopes. Parks department staff set up a temporary viewing area and asked visitors to keep a respectful distance so the bird is not disturbed.

"We're thrilled to see so many people getting outdoors and paying attention to the natural world right here in our neighborhood," said parks spokesperson Eli Carson. "Moments like this remind us how much wildlife passes through our city."

Ornithologists note that the tanager has been feeding on insects and berries in the grove and appears healthy. Experts advise that it may move on within days as conditions change.

Anyone hoping to catch a glimpse should visit the oak grove early in the morning, when birds are most active. Parks officials ask visitors not to use playback calls, which can stress wildlife.

**Rents Climb as Students Return to Maple Hollow**

Rent is rising faster than paychecks in Maple Hollow, and the university's fall enrollment surge is putting pressure on the town's housing market. According to a report released this week by the Maple Hollow Housing Coalition, the median one-bedroom apartment now rents for $1,640 a month, up 14 percent from a year ago.

"Two years ago, I could find a decent place near downtown for under $1,200," said Dana Whitfield, a graduate student in environmental science who has lived on Crestview Avenue since 2023. "This year, my landlord raised the rent $300 with a 30-day notice. I'm lucky I didn't have to leave."

Local property managers say the increases reflect higher demand. Enrollment at Maple Hollow State University reached 22,400 this semester, its highest total in a decade, while the number of available rental units has barely changed. Several new apartment complexes are under construction on the city's east side, but none will open before next summer.

City Council member Raymond Ortiz said the council will consider a proposal next month to ease zoning rules for accessory dwelling units, such as backyard cottages and converted garages. "We can't build our way out of this overnight," Ortiz said at Tuesday's meeting, "but we can give homeowners more options."

Tenant advocates are calling for stronger notice requirements and a cap on mid-lease increases. Landlords' representatives argue that property taxes, insurance, and maintenance costs have also climbed sharply, leaving little room to hold rents steady.

The university's housing office reports that its dormitories are full and that a waiting list of more than 600 students has formed for off-campus referrals. Students seeking housing are encouraged to contact the office before the spring application deadline.

**Riverbend Bridge to Close for Six-Month Repairs Starting January**

RIVERBEND, Nov. 18 — The Maple Street Bridge over the Tanner River will close to all traffic on January 5 for six months of structural repairs, city officials announced Tuesday.

Public Works Director Dana Whitfield said inspections earlier this year found deterioration in the bridge's support beams and deck joints. "The bridge is safe for now, but the damage has reached a point where waiting would only make the repairs more expensive and more disruptive," Whitfield said.

Crews will replace sections of the concrete deck, reinforce the north and south piers, and install new drainage. The project is expected to cost $14.2 million, funded through a state infrastructure grant and city bonds.

The closure will affect about 9,000 vehicles a day. Detour routes will send drivers across the Hollis Street Bridge, about two miles upstream, and along Route 9 through the Eastside industrial district. City officials warned that the detours will add roughly 15 minutes to a typical commute during peak hours.

Pedestrians and cyclists will have no direct crossing during the closure. The Riverbend Transit Authority will add a shuttle between the Downtown and Eastside stations, beginning January 5, with service every 20 minutes on weekdays.

Local businesses on the west side of the river expressed mixed feelings. Tom Okafor, owner of Okafor's Hardware on Maple Street, said he expects a drop in foot traffic but hopes the work will bring stability. "Nobody likes construction, but a bridge that holds up is better for everyone," he said.

Work is scheduled to finish by early July, weather permitting. Officials will post updates on the city website and send alerts through the RiverAlert text service.

Residents with questions can attend the public information session on December 3 at Riverbend Community Center, beginning at 6:30 p.m.

**Incumbent Holds Seat in Close Race for Riverbend Township Board**

RIVERBEND, Ohio (Nov. 18, 2026) - Incumbent Carol Whitfield won reelection to the Riverbend Township Board on Tuesday, defeating challenger Dale Ostrander by 214 votes, according to unofficial results released by the county board of elections.

Whitfield received 2,107 votes, or 51.3 percent, to Ostrander's 1,893. Voter turnout was 38 percent, slightly above the township's average for off-year elections.

"I'm grateful to every neighbor who came out to vote," Whitfield said Tuesday night at the township hall. "The past four years have been about fixing roads, keeping our fire station open and listening to residents. I plan to keep doing that."

Ostrander, a retired school maintenance supervisor, conceded the race Wednesday morning but said his campaign had raised concerns about drainage on Mill Creek Road and the township's budget process. "We got people talking about issues that matter here," he said. "I hope the board takes those concerns seriously."

The race was the only contested township board election this year. Voters also approved a 0.5-mill levy for road repairs, passing with 58 percent of the vote.

Provisional and absentee ballots will be counted over the next two weeks. Certification is scheduled for Dec. 2, and the county says final results could shift slightly, though officials do not expect the outcome to change.

Whitfield's new four-year term begins January 5.

**Museum Returns Ceremonial Mask to Community of Origin**

*Riverside Heritage Museum marks a milestone in restitution efforts*

RIVERSIDE — A carved ceremonial mask that has spent more than a century on display at the Riverside Heritage Museum will return to its homeland next spring, museum officials announced Tuesday.

The wooden mask, used in harvest celebrations by the Aruma community, was acquired in 1911 under circumstances the museum now acknowledges were exploitative. Its return is the latest step in a review of the institution's collection, which began in 2022 after pressure from community groups and academic researchers.

"This mask was made to be danced with, not locked behind glass," said Eleni Varga, the museum's director. "Returning it is the right thing to do, and it is long overdue."

Representatives from the Aruma Cultural Council traveled to Riverside last week to inspect the object and take part in a closing ceremony. Council chair Tomas Ruiz said the mask's return would help restore knowledge of traditional practices to younger generations.

"Our elders have spoken about this mask all our lives," Ruiz said. "To see it come home is a gift to our children."

The museum will cover shipping and conservation costs. A replica will be displayed in its place, accompanied by a panel explaining the mask's history and the agreement behind its return.

Visitors can view the mask until its departure date in March. Museum staff say they expect a large turnout for the final weeks of its display.

The museum has also begun reviewing about 300 other objects from the same region, with decisions expected in the coming year.

**Lincoln Ridge Middle School Bans Phones During Class Time**

*Hollis Falls, November 18, 2026*

Starting next Monday, students at Lincoln Ridge Middle School will no longer be able to use phones during class. Principal DeniseAr­royo announced the policy at Tuesday's school board meeting, saying teachers had reported growing distraction in classrooms.

# Registering a Birth

Registering a birth is a legal requirement and establishes your child's official identity. It also provides the documentation needed for healthcare, schooling, passports, and benefits. Please register your child's birth within the timeframe set by your local registration district, which is generally within 42 days in most areas.

## Who Can Register

The birth can usually be registered by:

- One of the child's parents
- A relative present at the birth
- The person in charge of the place where the birth occurred
- An authorized representative, such as a solicitor or agent

## What You Will Need

Please gather the following before your appointment:

- The child's medical birth notification, provided by the hospital or attending midwife
- Your identification, such as a passport or driver's licence
- Proof of address
- Parents' marriage certificate, if the parents are married
- Your National Insurance or Social Security number, if applicable

## How to Register

1. **Book an appointment** with your local registration office. Appointments are recommended and may be required.
2. **Attend in person** with the documents listed above.
3. **Check the details** on the birth certificate before you leave. Corrections are more complicated once the record is filed.
4. **Receive your certificate.** A short-form or full certificate can be requested at the time of registration, with additional copies available for a fee.

## Need Help?

If you have questions about your eligibility or the documents you need, please contact your local registration office or visit our website. Staff can advise you on the process and any applicable deadlines.

Registering a Birth

All births that occur in this country must be registered with the civil registration office within 30 days of the event. Registration creates the official record of your child's birth and is the basis for obtaining a birth certificate, a passport, and access to healthcare, schooling, and other public services.

Who should register

The parents of the child are responsible for registration. If the parents are unable to register, the responsibility passes to the person in charge of the place where the birth occurred, such as the hospital administrator, or to another adult with direct knowledge of the birth.

What you will need

Please gather the following before you visit the office or begin the online process. You will need the parents' identification documents, the medical certificate of birth issued by the attending healthcare provider, the marriage certificate if the parents are married, and proof of address. If you are registering a birth that took place at home, a statement from a witness may also be required.

How to register

Registration can be completed in person at any local registration office or, where available, through the agency's secure online portal. Appointments are recommended during busy periods. Once your application is accepted, you will receive a receipt, and certified copies of the birth certificate may be ordered for a small fee.

Late registration

Births not registered within 30 days may still be registered, but additional documentation and a sworn declaration may be required. Please contact your local office as soon as possible to avoid delays.

For further help, visit our website or call our public information line during office hours.

# Household Recycling Guidelines

Recycling keeps useful materials out of landfills and reduces the energy needed to make new products. Following a few simple rules helps ensure your recycling is collected and processed properly.

**What can go in your recycling bin**

- Clean, empty containers made of plastic, glass, metal, and cardboard
- Paper, including newspapers, magazines, and office paper
- Cardboard boxes, flattened and dry
- Aluminum cans and steel food tins

**What does not belong**

- Food waste, liquids, or greasy containers
- Plastic bags and film, which should be returned to a store drop-off bin
- Garden hoses, clothing, and textiles
- Batteries, electronics, and light bulbs, which require special disposal
- Pizza boxes with grease stains

**Preparing your items**

Rinse containers briefly to remove food residue. Remove lids from bottles and jars unless local rules say otherwise. Keep paper dry, and do not bag your recycling. Flatten boxes to save space in the bin.

**Special items**

Hazardous waste such as paint, chemicals, and batteries should be taken to a designated collection site. Bulky electronics can often be returned to retailers or scheduled for pickup through your local waste authority.

**Questions**

For details specific to your area, contact your municipal waste department or visit the local authority website. Rules vary by location, so check your collection calendar before placing items at the curb.

# Renewing a Passport for a Child

Keeping your child's passport current is important for travel. This page explains the basic steps for renewal.

## Who Must Apply in Person

Children under 16 must apply in person. Mailing in a renewal application is generally not an option for this age group. Bring the child to an acceptance facility or passport agency appointment.

## What to Bring

- **Form DS-11**, completed but not signed until you are before the acceptance agent
- **The child's current passport**, even if it is expired or damaged
- **A recent photo** that meets passport photo requirements
- **Proof of U.S. citizenship**, such as an original or certified birth certificate, if needed
- **Photo identification** for the parent or guardian presenting the application
- **Payment** for application and execution fees, which are listed on the official website

## Consent Requirements

Both parents or legal guardians should attend with the child. If one parent cannot attend, they must complete Form DS-3053, a signed statement of consent, and provide a copy of their photo identification. Court orders may also be required in certain custody situations.

## Processing Times

Processing times vary by season and demand. Check the official website for current estimates. If you have upcoming travel, apply well in advance, and consider expedited service if needed.

## Important Reminders

- Passports are generally valid for 10 years for applicants age 16 and older, and 5 years for children under 16.
- Make sure your child's passport has at least six months of validity remaining before international travel.
- Avoid unofficial websites that charge extra fees. Only use official government resources.

For the most current forms, fees, and locations, visit the official agency website or call the customer contact center.

# Food Hygiene Ratings: What They Mean for You

Food hygiene ratings help you choose where to eat with confidence. Every food business inspected by our agency receives a rating that reflects how well it handles, prepares, and stores food, and how clean its premises are.

## How Ratings Work

Ratings are based on an inspection of three areas:

- **Hygienic food handling:** how food is cooked, cooled, reheated, and kept at safe temperatures
- **Structural condition:** the cleanliness and maintenance of floors, walls, ceilings, and equipment
- **Management of food safety:** staff training, record-keeping, and procedures to prevent contamination

Each business is given a rating on a scale from 0 to 5, where 5 means very good hygiene standards and 0 means urgent improvement is necessary.

## Checking a Rating

Ratings are published online and displayed on a sticker at the entrance of many food businesses. Search by business name or postcode to view the latest result and inspection date.

## Why Ratings Can Change

Ratings reflect conditions on the day of inspection. A business may improve or decline between visits. Inspections are carried out regularly, and businesses can request a re-inspection once they have made improvements.

## Raising a Concern

If you are worried about a food business, you can report it to us. We take every report seriously and will investigate where needed.

## Learn More

For guidance on safe food practices at home or in business, visit our website or contact our public information team.

**What to Do If You Lose Your Job**

Losing a job is stressful, but there are steps you can take to protect your finances and access support.

**1. Confirm your separation details.**
Ask your former employer for a written notice stating your last day of work, your final pay, and any severance terms. Keep copies of all documents.

**2. Collect your final pay and benefits information.**
Your final paycheck should include wages earned through your last day, and possibly unused paid time off, depending on your state's rules. Ask how to continue health coverage, such as through COBRA, and note the deadline to enroll.

**3. File for unemployment insurance.**
Apply as soon as possible through your state's unemployment insurance agency, since benefits are generally not paid retroactively. Have your Social Security number, employment history, and last employer's contact information ready. Continue to certify your eligibility as your state requires, even if you are looking for work.

**4. Check your retirement accounts.**
If you have a 401(k) or similar plan, review your options before withdrawing funds. Rolling the balance into an IRA or a new employer's plan can help you avoid taxes and penalties.

**5. Create a budget.**
List essential expenses such as housing, utilities, food, and transportation. Identify ways to reduce costs and contact creditors early if you expect payment difficulties.

**6. Get help finding work.**
Visit your local American Job Center for free career counseling, job search workshops, and training resources. Search for openings at USAJOBS.gov for federal positions.

**7. Protect yourself from scams.**
Be cautious of job offers that ask for payment or personal financial information. Legitimate employers do not charge fees to apply.

For more information, contact your state workforce agency or visit the official government benefits website for your state.

Stopping a dog from pulling on the lead takes consistency, but it's very achievable. Here's what works:

**1. Stop moving when he pulls.** As soon as the lead goes tight, stand still. Walk forward again only when the lead goes slack. Dogs learn that pulling gets them nowhere.

**2. Reward loose-lead walking.** Keep treats handy and reward him whenever he's beside you or the lead is loose. Mark the moment with a "yes!" and deliver the treat quickly.

**3. Change direction.** If he forges ahead, turn and walk the other way, calling him or patting your leg to encourage him to follow. Reward him when he catches up.

**4. Use the right equipment.** A front-clip harness (such as a Freedom No-Pull or similar) gives you more control without harming his neck. Avoid choke or prong collars unless guided by a qualified trainer.

**5. Practise in low-distraction areas first.** Start in your garden or a quiet street, then gradually work up to busier places.

**6. Keep sessions short.** Five to ten minutes of focused practice, several times a day, works better than one long session.

Be patient. Most dogs take several weeks of consistent practice to become reliable. If progress stalls, a positive-reinforcement trainer can give tailored help.

Sand it first, or at least scuff it. Gloss paint is slick, and new paint won't grip it well. Without preparation, you risk peeling, chipping, and blotchy sheen.

Here's the usual approach:

1. **Clean the surface.** Wash it with a degreaser such as TSP (or a substitute) to remove grease, dust, and grime, then rinse and let it dry.
2. **Scuff sand.** Use 120–220 grit to dull the gloss. You don't need to remove all the old paint, just rough up the surface evenly.
3. **Fill and sand any damage.** Patch chips or dents, then sand smooth.
4. **Wipe off the dust.** A tack cloth works well.
5. **Prime.** Use a bonding primer, especially if you're switching from oil to latex or going to a much lighter or darker color.
6. **Paint** with your topcoat.

If you skip sanding, a liquid deglosser or bonding primer can work, but sanding is more reliable.

If the house was built before 1978, test for lead paint before sanding. Lead dust is hazardous, so use a test kit and wet-sand or use proper dust controls if it's positive.

I had the same fear for about two years, so I get it. What helped me most was going slowly and in small steps. I started on quiet A-roads, then did one junction onto a motorway at a time, always at a quiet hour like Sunday morning. Stay in the left lane until you feel settled, and don't worry about keeping up with the traffic. Plenty of people cruise at 60 and nobody cares.

Having a calm passenger along for the first few runs made a big difference too. And if the panic is bad, a driving instructor who specialises in nervous drivers is worth paying for. They can sit with you on the slip roads and show you exactly what to do with your hands and eyes when you're merging, which takes a lot of the mystery out of it.

Give yourself permission to take a break and pull into a services if you need one. Most of the fear fades once you've done it a few times and realise nothing dramatic happens.

Yes, you can use olive oil to season cast iron, and it works well. Olive oil has a lower smoke point than some alternatives, so keep the heat moderate to avoid a sticky, smoky mess.

Here's how:

1. **Clean the pan.** Wash it with warm water and a little mild soap, then dry it completely. Heat it on the stove for a few minutes to evaporate any leftover moisture.
2. **Apply a thin layer.** Rub a small amount of olive oil over the entire pan, inside and out, then wipe off as much as you can. The pan should look dry, not glossy. Too much oil leads to a tacky finish.
3. **Bake it.** Place the pan upside down in a 450–475°F (230–245°C) oven for about an hour. Put a sheet of foil on the rack below to catch drips.
4. **Let it cool** in the oven with the heat off.

Repeat the thin coat and bake cycle two or three times for a durable base. Some people prefer flaxseed or grapeseed oil because they polymerize well at high heat, but olive oil is a perfectly good choice for everyday seasoning. Avoid extra-virgin oil for the first layers if you can, since it may smoke more, though refined olive oil works fine.

The best method depends on the herb.

**Soft herbs (basil, cilantro, parsley, mint, dill):** Treat them like cut flowers. Trim the stem ends, stand them in a glass of water on the counter or in the fridge, and cover loosely with a plastic bag. Change the water every couple of days. Basil is the exception: keep it at room temperature, since cold damages it.

**Hardy herbs (rosemary, thyme, sage, oregano):** Wrap the stems in a barely damp paper towel, place them in a loosely closed plastic bag or container, and refrigerate. They often last 1 to 3 weeks this way.

**Freezing:** Chop herbs and pack them into ice cube trays with a little water or olive oil. Once frozen, transfer the cubes to a bag. This works well for cilantro, parsley, basil, and chives, though they lose their texture, so use them in cooked dishes.

**Drying:** Hang small bundles upside down in a dry, dark spot for one to two weeks, or use a dehydrator on low. Store them in airtight jars away from light. Dried herbs keep flavor for about six months to a year.

Avoid washing herbs until you're ready to use them, since moisture speeds up spoilage.

Fungus gnats usually appear because the soil stays too wet. The adult gnats are harmless flyers, but their larvae live in the top layer of soil and feed on organic matter and tender roots, so they're worth controlling.

**Common causes:**
- **Overwatering.** Gnats lay eggs in moist soil, and the larvae thrive in soggy conditions. This is the most frequent cause.
- **Poor drainage.** Pots without drainage holes, or dense soil, hold water too long.
- **Decaying organic matter.** Fallen leaves, dead plant debris, or peat-heavy mixes that stay damp can attract them.
- **Contaminated soil or new plants.** Gnats often arrive in bagged soil or on newly purchased plants.

**How to fix it:**
1. **Let the top 1–2 inches of soil dry out** before watering again.
2. **Water from the bottom** or let excess water drain fully. Empty saucers.
3. **Remove debris** and any moldy material from the soil surface.
4. **Use yellow sticky traps** to catch adults and reduce breeding.
5. **Try a BTI product** (Bti, sold as "Mosquito Dunks" or gnat-specific formulas). It's safe for pets and kills larvae in the soil.
6. **Repot if needed** using fresh, well-draining potting mix.

With consistent drying between waterings, most infestations clear up within a few weeks.

Try these in order, starting with the least invasive:

1. **Rubber band or steel wool:** Press a wide rubber band or a pad of steel wool into the screw head, then firmly seat your driver. The extra grip is often enough.

2. **Tighten and loosen slowly:** Apply firm downward pressure while turning very slowly. Sometimes a bit of pressure is all it takes to bite.

3. **Cut a new slot:** Use a rotary tool or hacksaw to cut a straight slot across the head, then turn it with a flathead screwdriver.

4. **Hammer-in extractor:** Tap a left-hand spiral extractor bit into a center-punched hole, then turn counterclockwise. Drill a pilot hole first if needed.

5. **Drill it out:** Use a bit slightly smaller than the screw's shank to drill out the center, then remove the remaining threads with an screw extractor or pliers.

Tips: Use a bit that fits the screw snugly, and penetrating oil helps if the screw is corroded. If the screw is in a delicate surface, stop and use a more controlled method to avoid damage.

The general guideline for rest between sets is 2 to 5 minutes for most lifting, depending on your goal and the exercise.

- **Strength (heavy, 1–5 reps):** Rest 3–5 minutes. Heavy compound lifts like squats, deadlifts, and bench press need full recovery to keep your force output high.
- **Hypertrophy (muscle growth, 6–12 reps):** Rest about 1–3 minutes. Shorter rests work well, though longer rests on heavy sets can help you hit good reps.
- **Endurance (15+ reps):** Rest 30–90 seconds, since these sets are less taxing on the nervous system.

Smaller isolation exercises, like bicep curls or lateral raises, usually need less rest than big compound lifts. If you're still breathing hard or your next set's reps are clearly dropping, take a bit longer. The best guide is your performance: rest until you can lift the next set with good form and close to your target reps.

It depends a lot on which two languages and where you are at with them. If they're pretty different, like Japanese and Spanish, the overlap is small and you probably won't mix them up much. If they're close, like Spanish and Portuguese, or Norwegian and Swedish, your brain will keep swapping words, and that can be annoying for a while.

The real problem is usually time, not interference. Splitting an hour a day between two languages means each one moves more slowly, and it's easy to feel like you're making no progress in either.

What tends to work: pick one as the main language and give it most of your time. Use the second one for something lighter, like a daily podcast, a few flashcards, or one short conversation a week. Once the first one feels comfortable, switch the balance if you want.

Also, if you're learning them for different reasons, like work and travel, that's a good reason to keep both going. If you're just doing it because it sounds impressive, I'd start with one.

Check the frame first. Look for cracks, dents, or creases, especially around the head tube, bottom bracket, and seat tube, and sight down the top tube for kinks. Carbon frames need extra scrutiny: tap the frame lightly with a coin and listen for a dull thud, which can signal delamination.

Next, check the drivetrain. Shift through every gear. Worn chains skip under load, and a chain stretched past 0.75% wear needs replacing, which costs about $30 to $50. Cassettes and chainrings with hooked, shark-fin teeth mean the whole drivetrain is due for replacement.

Test the brakes and wheels. Spin each wheel and watch for wobble or rubbing. Squeeze the brake levers, and make sure the pads have plenty of material left.

Check the headset by rocking the front wheel while braking. Clunking or looseness suggests it needs adjusting or replacing. Feel for rough or gritty bearings as you turn the bars.

Ask for the bike's history and a fit check. A bike that's too small or too large is hard to fix, so confirm the frame size matches your height and inseam. Also ask whether the bike was crashed or used in wet conditions.

Finally, get a test ride on a route that includes hills and rough pavement, and consider a pre-purchase inspection at a local bike shop, typically $50 to $100.

Bread crust goes soft because of moisture. A crust is dry and crisp when it loses water to the air. Once it's exposed to humidity, it reabsorbs moisture from the crumb and the air, and it softens.

Common causes:

- **Storing it too early.** Bread that's cut or stored while still warm releases steam that gets trapped and softens the crust.
- **Wrapping it while it's still hot or warm.** Plastic bags trap moisture. Let loaves cool fully, around 2 to 4 hours, before bagging.
- **Storing in a humid place.** Kitchens with steam, dishwashers, or a damp counter speed this up.
- **Refrigerating.** Fridges can make bread stale faster, and they don't keep crust crisp.

Fixes:

- Cool the loaf completely on a wire rack before cutting or storing.
- Store it cut side down on a board, or in a paper bag or bread box, for a day or two.
- For a crisp crust again, reheat the loaf at 350°F (175°C) for 5 to 10 minutes, then let it cool briefly.
- Freeze slices you won't eat within a couple of days.

Bread crust goes soft because it absorbs moisture from the inside of the loaf and from the air around it. Right after baking, the crust is dry and crisp, but the interior releases steam for hours. That steam condenses on the crust, softening it.

Storage makes this worse. A plastic bag traps moisture and turns a crisp crust soft within an hour or two. Refrigeration speeds up starch retrogradation, which also makes bread stale faster.

To keep the crust crisp, let the loaf cool completely on a wire rack before cutting or storing it, since cutting early lets steam escape unevenly. Store it cut side down on a cutting board, or in a paper bag or bread box, which lets some moisture escape while protecting it from drying out. If the crust has already softened, reheat the loaf in a 300°F (150°C) oven for 5 to 10 minutes, then let it cool briefly before eating.

Rent. For one week of lessons, renting is almost always the better deal. Many surf schools include a wetsuit in the lesson price, so check that first, since you may not need to pay separately at all.

Renting also means you don't have to guess the right thickness before you know the local water temperature. A shop can usually match you to the conditions: a 3/2mm suit for warm water, a 4/3mm for mid-range temperatures, and a 5/4mm or thicker for cold water. Ask the shop to check the fit in the store, since a suit that's too loose lets in cold water and one that's too tight restricts your paddling.

If you're still surfing after the week and plan to keep going, you can buy a suit later, once you know your preferred thickness and fit. A well-fitting suit is worth the investment then, but buying one before you've had any lessons usually means paying for something you may not use the way you expected.

**Pothos** is one of the best first houseplants for a dark flat. It tolerates low light, forgives missed waterings, and trails or climbs attractively.

Snake plants and ZZ plants are also excellent. Both store water in their leaves or rhizomes, so they handle neglect well, and they grow slowly in dim conditions.

Some tips for low light:

- **Water less than you think.** Overwatering kills more indoor plants than underwatering. Let the top few centimetres of soil dry out before watering again. Lower light means slower drying.
- **Place plants as close to a window as you can**, ideally one that gets some daylight, even if it's indirect.
- **Skip fertiliser** until spring and summer, since plants grow very little in winter gloom.
- **Wipe leaves occasionally** with a damp cloth so they can absorb more light.

Pothos will show you when something's wrong: yellowing leaves usually mean too much water, while crispy edges suggest it needs a drink. Start with one plant, learn its signals, and you'll find it easier to add more.

Start small and make it easy to do. Set a time, like right after your morning coffee or before bed, and write for five minutes. Don't aim for pages. A few honest sentences count.

Use a prompt if a blank page stops you. Try "What's on my mind today?", "What went well, and what was hard?", or "What am I grateful for?" Prompts give you a starting point.

Keep the bar low. Missing a day isn't failure. Just start again the next day without guilt or catching up. Don't reread old entries or worry about spelling, grammar, or whether it's "good" writing. Nobody else needs to read it.

Keep the journal where you'll see it. A notebook on your nightstand works better than an app buried in your phone, or the reverse if you type faster. Some people pair journaling with an existing habit, like writing after they make tea.

Track the habit, not the content. A simple streak on a calendar can motivate you. If you miss several days in a row, ask what got in the way. Adjust the time, length, or format instead of quitting.

Finally, give it a month. The habit usually starts to feel automatic after a few weeks of showing up, even on messy days.

Usually it's not your app. It's everything the image carries along with it.

The biggest culprit is the base image. `python:3.12` or `node:20` are full Debian images with compilers, headers, and tooling, and they can easily be 900 MB before you've copied anything. Switching to the `-slim` tag, or to alpine or distroless if your app can handle it, often cuts a huge chunk.

Next, check what you're copying in. A bare `COPY . .` pulls in `.git`, local virtualenvs, test fixtures, sample data, and whatever else is sitting in your project folder. A `.dockerignore` fixes most of that.

Dependencies are another common source. Installing build tools with apt and leaving them in place, or skipping the `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` step, adds up. For pip, use `--no-cache-dir`. For npm, install only production dependencies in the final stage.

The one that trips people up most is deleting files in a later layer. Docker layers are additive, so if you download a 300 MB archive in one `RUN`, then delete it in the next, the image still contains it. Do the download, use, and cleanup in the same `RUN` command.

If you want the real answer, run `docker history <image>` to see which layers are big, or try `dive`, which lets you browse each layer's contents. Multi-stage builds, where you compile in one stage and copy only the output into a slim runtime stage, solve most of this.

Short answer: use auto-increment integers unless you have a specific reason not to. Long answer below.

**Use auto-increment (BIGINT) IDs when:**
- All data lives in one database, and you don't need IDs before inserting.
- You want compact indexes and fast joins. Integers are smaller and more cache-friendly than UUIDs.
- IDs are rarely exposed to users. If they are, sequential IDs leak information like row counts and invite enumeration, so pair them with authorization checks.

**Use UUIDs when:**
- You generate IDs in clients or across services and need them before the database assigns anything.
- You merge data from multiple databases or shards and need globally unique keys.
- You want to hide record counts or make URLs non-guessable.

**Trade-offs for UUIDs:**
- Random UUIDv4 values scatter inserts across B-tree indexes, which hurts write performance and bloats indexes. Use time-ordered variants like UUIDv7 or ULID to mitigate this.
- They take 16 bytes versus 4 or 8, which adds up in large tables and in every foreign key.

**A common compromise:** use a sequential integer as the internal primary key and add a separate UUID column for external references. This keeps joins fast and avoids exposing sequential IDs.

Laptop battery drain in sleep is usually caused by something keeping the system partly awake. Common culprits:

- **Wake events:** Check what's waking it. On Linux, look at `/proc/acpi/wakeup` and `journalctl -b -1 | grep -i wake`. On Windows, run `powercfg -lastwake`. On macOS, check `pmset -g log | grep -i wake`. USB devices, network cards (Wake-on-LAN), and lid or keyboard sensors are frequent causes.
- **Network activity:** Background sync, Wi-Fi scans, or push notifications can keep the NIC active. Disabling Wake-on-LAN or setting Wi-Fi to sleep when idle often helps.
- **Suspend-to-RAM vs. hibernate:** Pure S3 sleep should draw only a few percent per day. If you're seeing a large drop, try hibernate-on-sleep or a hybrid mode with a timeout (on Windows, `powercfg /hibernate on` and set the hybrid sleep timeout).
- **Drivers and firmware:** GPU, Thunderbolt, and Bluetooth drivers are common offenders. Check for BIOS/UEFI updates.
- **Kernel or OS bugs:** On Linux, try `systemd-analyze` and check `cat /sys/power/mem_sleep`. Setting `mem_sleep` to `deep` can reduce drain on some hardware.

Yes, SQLite can work well in production for a small app, but it depends on your workload.

It's a good fit when:
- You have a single server (or one app instance) and no need to scale horizontally.
- Writes are modest. SQLite allows one writer at a time, though WAL mode handles concurrent reads well.
- You want simple backups, low operational overhead, and no separate database process.

Some things to get right:
- Enable WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;`) and set a busy timeout so writers wait instead of failing.
- Back up with the `.backup` command or the online backup API, not by copying the file while it's in use.
- Keep the database on local disk. Network filesystems like NFS can corrupt it.
- Use a connection pool sized for SQLite, typically few writers.

Move to PostgreSQL or MySQL if you need multiple app servers writing to the same data, heavy concurrent write traffic, or features like advanced replication or per-user access control.

For most small apps with one server, SQLite is simpler and more reliable than people expect. Start with it, measure, and migrate only if you hit its limits.

Don't roll your own. Use a slow, salted password hash that's built for this: Argon2id if your library supports it, otherwise bcrypt or scrypt. Most frameworks have one built in, so just use that. The salt gets generated and stored for you, and you should tune the work factor so a single hash takes maybe 100-300ms on your server.

Never store plaintext, and don't use reversible encryption for passwords. You never need to get the original password back, only to check a guess against the hash. If your DB leaks, encrypted passwords are one key-file away from being readable.

Other stuff that matters more than people think:

- Don't log passwords, even in debug output or error traces.
- Rate limit login attempts and add some lockout or backoff.
- Offer MFA, especially for admins.
- Check new passwords against breached-password lists (the HIBP k-anonymity API works fine) instead of enforcing silly composition rules.
- A pepper (secret key kept outside the DB) is a nice extra layer, but it's not a substitute for the hash.

SQLite is a solid choice for a small app, and it's more capable in production than many people assume. It handles read-heavy workloads well, runs in-process with no network hop, and needs no separate server to patch or monitor. Backups are as simple as copying the file or using the .backup command while the app runs.

The main limits are write concurrency and multi-host deployment. SQLite allows only one writer at a time, so turn on WAL mode and set a busy timeout to avoid "database is locked" errors. Keep transactions short. If you need several app servers writing to the same data, or heavy concurrent writes, move to PostgreSQL.

Put the database file on local disk, not NFS or a network share, since file locking over the network is unreliable. Run regular backups and test restoring them. Set file permissions so only the app user can read the file.

For a single-server app with modest traffic, SQLite is often the simpler and more reliable option. Start with it, and migrate only when you hit a real limit.

Usually it's a authentication or reputation problem, and the fix is mostly DNS configuration. Check these first:

1. **SPF, DKIM, and DMARC:** Make sure your domain has an SPF record that lists every server allowed to send for it, DKIM signing enabled, and a DMARC policy (even `p=none` to start). Missing or misaligned records are the most common cause.
2. **Reverse DNS (PTR):** If you're sending from your own server, the sending IP's PTR record should resolve to a hostname that matches your mail server's HELO/EHLO name.
3. **IP and domain reputation:** Check your sending IP against Spamhaus, Barracuda, and SpamCop. A shared or previously abused IP can get blocked. Check your domain on Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS.
4. **Content and links:** Heavy HTML, image-only messages, URL shorteners, or links to flagged domains can trigger filters. Include a plain-text version and avoid spammy phrasing.
5. **Engagement:** Gmail and Outlook weigh recipient behavior. Low open rates or many "mark as spam" reports push future mail to the spam folder.
6. **Bounce and complaint rates:** Sending to old or invalid addresses hurts reputation. Remove bounces promptly.

To diagnose, send a test to a Gmail account, open "Show original," and read the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results. Also, mail-tester.com gives a quick score and specific warnings.

Yes, almost always. On an old PC, an SSD is usually the single biggest performance upgrade you can make.

The main reason is random I/O. Spinning disks handle sequential reads well but struggle with the many small, scattered reads an OS and applications generate. Boot times, application launches, and file searches that crawl on an HDD often feel several times faster on an SSD. Even a cheap SATA SSD makes an old machine feel responsive again.

Things to consider:

- **Interface:** A SATA SSD works in nearly any PC from the last 15 years. An NVMe drive only helps if your motherboard has an M.2 slot that supports it, and it won't matter much on a very old system.
- **Capacity:** You can clone your existing drive or do a fresh install. Cloning is easier if you want to keep your setup.
- **Cost:** Prices are low, so a 500 GB to 1 TB SATA SSD is a reasonable choice.
- **Keep the HDD:** Old hard drives are useful for bulk storage like media or backups.

Bottom line: if the machine is still worth using, the SSD is worth it. If the CPU, RAM, or OS is badly limited, consider upgrading those too, but the SSD will still help the most per dollar.

A load average of 4 on a 4-core server means, on average, four processes were either running on a CPU or waiting for one over the sampled period. Since you have four cores, each core was roughly 100% busy with no queue building up. That's a healthy, fully utilized machine, not an overloaded one.

The rule of thumb is to compare load average to core count:

- **Below the core count:** some capacity is idle.
- **Equal to the core count:** the system is at full capacity.
- **Above the core count:** work is queuing. A load of 8 on 4 cores means about twice as many runnable tasks as cores, so each task waits roughly half its time.

Keep in mind that Linux load average also counts processes in uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on disk or NFS I/O. So a high load doesn't always mean high CPU use. Check `top`, `vmstat`, or `iostat` to see whether the CPU or I/O is the bottleneck.

The three numbers from `uptime` are averages over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Comparing them shows whether load is rising, falling, or steady.

Regional slowness usually comes down to network path, CDN coverage, or where your origin server sits. Start by checking these:

1. **Origin location:** If your server is in the US or Europe, every request from Asia crosses long undersea routes, which adds 150–300 ms or more per round trip. Multiply that by the number of requests and the page feels slow.
2. **CDN coverage:** Confirm your CDN has Asian points of presence and that they're actually serving your assets. Check whether a CDN edge is being bypassed by a hardcoded origin URL or a misconfigured DNS record.
3. **Routing:** Run `mtr` or `traceroute` from an Asian vantage point (or use a multi-region tool like Pingdom, WebPageTest, or Catchpoint). Look for high latency or packet loss at a specific hop, which can point to a congested peering link.
4. **Blocking or throttling:** Some regions have aggressive filtering or rate limiting. Check your WAF and bot-protection logs for challenges or blocks coming from Asian IP ranges.
5. **Uncached dynamic responses:** If HTML isn't cached, every visitor hits the origin. Add caching headers where appropriate.
6. **Third-party scripts:** Analytics, fonts, or ad tags that are slow in certain regions can block rendering. Test with them disabled.

A VPN and a proxy both route your traffic through an intermediate server, but they work at different layers and offer different protection.

A **proxy** typically forwards traffic for specific applications or protocols. An HTTP or SOCKS proxy only handles what you configure it to handle, so your browser might use one while other apps connect directly. It generally doesn't encrypt the whole connection, and the proxy operator can see and log your traffic.

A **VPN** creates an encrypted tunnel at the network level, usually through a virtual network interface. It routes all or most of your device's traffic, including DNS in a properly configured setup, through the VPN server. Your ISP sees only encrypted traffic to the VPN endpoint, and the VPN provider can still see your traffic unless you trust them not to log it.

In short:

- **Scope:** Proxy covers selected apps; VPN covers the whole device.
- **Encryption:** VPNs encrypt by default; most proxies don't.
- **Setup:** Proxies are often per-app and easy to configure; VPNs usually need a client and system-level routing.
- **Use case:** Proxies suit scraping, load balancing, or content routing. VPNs suit privacy on untrusted networks and securing all traffic.

Neither one makes you anonymous by itself. Your provider or proxy operator still sees where you connect, so choose one you trust.

- **Great Firewall**, if any of your users are in mainland China. Connections can be throttled or dropped there, and it looks like "slow" more than "down."

# pngsquash

**pngsquash** is a fast, lossless command-line tool for shrinking PNG files. It re-encodes images with optimized compression settings, strips unnecessary metadata, and reduces file size without changing a single pixel. Point it at one file, a directory, or a glob pattern, and it will rewrite your images in place or write them to a separate output folder.

Designed for developers, designers, and anyone who manages large image libraries, pngsquash fits neatly into build pipelines, pre-commit hooks, and batch scripts. It processes files in parallel, reports the savings for each image, and never overwrites a file unless the result is actually smaller.

A **webhook** is an automated message that one application sends to another when a specific event happens. Instead of your product repeatedly checking for updates, it pushes the relevant information to a URL you specify as soon as the event occurs.

For example, if you connect a payment provider to your account, the provider can send a webhook to your system whenever a payment succeeds, a subscription renews, or a refund is issued. Your system can then update orders, send confirmation emails, or trigger other actions in real time.

To use a webhook, you typically:

1. **Create an endpoint** on your server that can receive HTTP POST requests.
2. **Register the endpoint's URL** in the product's settings.
3. **Choose the events** you want to be notified about.
4. **Verify each request** using the signing secret provided, to confirm it genuinely came from the product.

# Appointments API

The Appointments API lets you book, reschedule, and cancel appointments with providers in your organization. Use it to build booking flows into your website, mobile app, or internal scheduling tools.

Each appointment ties together a **provider**, a **service**, a **client**, and a **time slot**. The API checks provider availability in real time, so a successful booking response means the slot is reserved for the client.

## What you can do

- **Check availability** for a provider and service across a date range.
- **Book an appointment** into an open slot.
- **Reschedule or cancel** existing appointments, with optional notifications to the client.
- **Retrieve appointment history** for a client or provider.

## Base URL

```
https://api.example.com/v1
```

All requests and responses use JSON. Send requests over HTTPS only.

## Authentication

Authenticate each request with a bearer token in the `Authorization` header:

```
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

Keep API keys server-side. Do not embed them in client-side code.

## App won't start

If the app opens to nothing, crashes right away, or just sits there with no window, work through these in order. Most of the time it's one of the first three.

**1. Restart your computer.** This sounds lazy, but it clears stuck background processes and locked files that keep the app from launching. If the app is still running invisibly, it can block the new instance.

**2. Check for a stuck process.** Sometimes the app is running but has no visible window, and the next launch just quits. On Windows, open Task Manager and end any leftover process with the app's name. On macOS, open Activity Monitor and do the same. On Linux, run `pkill -f appname` (swap in the real process name).

**3. Update the app.** If you haven't updated in a while, the version you have may not work with your current OS. Grab the latest installer from the download page, not the in-app updater, since the updater is often what broke in the first place.

**4. Reinstall cleanly.** Uninstall the app, then delete its leftover config folder before reinstalling. That folder is usually at:

- Windows: `%APPDATA%\AppName`
- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/AppName`
- Linux: `~/.config/appname`

Deleting it resets your settings, so back up anything you care about first. A corrupted settings file is a common cause of startup crashes.

**5. Run it from a terminal.** If the app still won't open, launch it from a terminal so you can see the error. On Windows, open Command Prompt in the install folder and run the `.exe`. On macOS, run the binary inside the `.app` bundle at `AppName.app/Contents/MacOS/AppName`. Copy whatever error prints out. It usually names the missing file or the problem outright.

**6. Check your graphics drivers.** Some desktop apps fail to start when the GPU driver is old or misbehaving. Update your graphics driver through the manufacturer's site or your OS update tool. If you can't update it right now, try launching with hardware acceleration turned off. Many apps accept a flag like `--disable-gpu` for this.

**7. Check your logs.** Most apps write a log file when they crash. Look in the same config folder from step 4, or search the app's support docs for "log location." The last few lines before the crash are usually the most useful.

If none of this works, send the support team the error text from step 5, your OS version, and the app version. Those three things get you a faster answer than "it doesn't open."

# Troubleshooting: App Won't Start

If the application does not launch, work through the steps below in order. Most startup failures come from a corrupted settings or cache file, a missing dependency, a blocked port or lock file, or an incompatible system requirement.

## 1. Confirm System Requirements

- Check that your operating system version is supported. See the minimum requirements in the release notes or installation guide.
- Verify that you have enough free disk space (at least 500 MB recommended) and available memory.
- Make sure your graphics drivers are up to date, since many desktop apps fail to start when GPU acceleration initializes incorrectly.

## 2. Restart and Check for Running Instances

- Fully quit the application, including any background or tray process. On Windows, check Task Manager. On macOS, check Activity Monitor. On Linux, run `ps aux | grep <appname>`.
- Terminate any leftover processes, then try launching again.
- Restart your computer if the app still will not open. This clears stale lock files and hung processes.

## 3. Launch from a Terminal to Read Error Output

Starting the app from a terminal often shows the error that the GUI hides:

- **Windows:** Open Command Prompt or PowerShell, navigate to the install folder, and run the executable.
- **macOS:** Run `/Applications/<AppName>.app/Contents/MacOS/<AppName>` in Terminal.
- **Linux:** Run the executable name or path directly in a terminal.

Note any error messages, especially those mentioning missing libraries, permissions, or ports.

## 4. Check Log Files

Most desktop apps write logs to a standard location:

- **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\<AppName>\logs`
- **macOS:** `~/Library/Logs/<AppName>`
- **Linux:** `~/.config/<AppName>/logs` or `~/.local/share/<AppName>/logs`

Open the most recent log file and look for lines marked `ERROR`, `FATAL`, or `Exception`.

## 5. Reset Settings and Cache

A corrupted configuration file is a common cause of startup crashes.

1. Quit the application completely.
2. Rename (do not delete yet) the configuration and cache folders:
   - **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\<AppName>` and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\<AppName>`
   - **macOS:** `~/Library/Application Support/<AppName>` and `~/Library/Caches/<AppName>`
   - **Linux:** `~/.config/<AppName>` and `~/.cache/<AppName>`
3. Launch the app again. It will recreate default settings.
4. If it starts, reapply your preferences manually or restore individual settings files from the renamed folder.

## 6. Remove Stale Lock or Socket Files

If the app reports that it is "already running" when it is not, a lock file may remain. Delete any files named `*.lock`, `lockfile`, or `*.pid` in the application data folder while the app is closed.

## 7. Check for Port Conflicts

Some apps use a local port for their internal server. If another program is using that port, startup will fail.

- Check the port number in the logs.
- Find the process using it:
  - **Windows:** `netstat -ano | findstr :<port>`
  - **macOS/Linux:** `lsof -i :<port>`
- Stop the conflicting process or change the app's port in its configuration.

## 8. Repair or Reinstall

If the steps above do not resolve the problem:

1. **Repair:** Use the installer's repair option if available (Windows: Apps & Features > Modify).
2. **Reinstall:** Uninstall the application, restart your computer, and install the latest version from the official source. Verify the download checksum if one is provided.
3. **Clean reinstall:** After uninstalling, remove any leftover data folders from Step 5 before installing again.

## 9. Check Permissions and Security Software

- Make sure your user account has read and write access to the install directory and the data folders.
- On macOS, go to System Settings > Privacy & Security and allow the app if it was blocked as an unidentified developer. On Windows, check whether Windows Defender SmartScreen or a third-party antivirus has quarantined files.
- On Linux, confirm the executable has permission to run (`chmod +x <file>`).

## 10. Gather Information Before Contacting Support

If you still cannot start the application, collect the following before filing a support request:

- Application version and build number
- Operating system and version
- Hardware details (CPU, GPU, RAM)
- The exact error message and the relevant log excerpt
- Steps you have already tried

Every engineering team has a crontab that nobody wants to touch. It started as one line, a nightly script to send reminder emails, and over the years it grew into thirty entries, some with comments that say "don't remove, Dana knows why," and a few that have been silently failing since March. We had all of those, and last quarter we decided to move them onto a job queue.

This post covers why we made that change, what we gave up along the way, and what we'd do differently. Cron is a fine tool for a single machine running a single task on a schedule. Our problem was that we had quietly asked it to be something else: a retry system, a record of what ran, a way to spread work across hosts, and an alerting pipeline. It does none of those things well, and we had been compensating with shell scripts, log greps, and tribal knowledge.

Moving to a queue-backed worker model meant rethinking jobs as units of work with explicit state. Each job now has an identity, a retry policy, a timeout, and a visible history. Failures show up where we can see them instead of in an inbox nobody reads. The migration was not free. We had to make every job idempotent, deal with duplicate deliveries, and decide which of those thirty cron entries actually still mattered. About a third of them turned out to be dead.

Below, we walk through the design, the migration steps, the mistakes we made, and the metrics we use to decide whether it worked.
